_meta.purpose: AIUC-1 (Q4-2026 release) in CatalogFile shape, so applyCatalogFile creates the framework, its 50 requirements, one control template per requirement, their requirement links and the pack together.
_meta.grounding: Requirement codes, titles, sections and summaries are generated from src/data/libraries/aiuc-1.yaml, so the library import and this catalogue write identical requirement rows. Every template — title, description, objective, successCriteria, testingMethodology and all task content — is authored in this repo from what each requirement asks an organisation to demonstrate.
_meta.grain: One template per AIUC-1 requirement. AIUC-1 audits each requirement on its own cadence and lets each be scoped in or out separately, so a requirement is the unit an auditor tests and the unit a tenant marks applicable; bundling them would force one frequency and one test plan onto requirements AIUC-1 evidences on different cycles.

framework.name: AIUC-1 AI Agent Standard
framework.description: AIUC-1 is a certification standard for AI agents, organised into six domains — data and privacy, security, safety, reliability, accountability and society — and audited by accredited auditors against what an agent can actually do, how it is built and where it runs. It is revised every quarter. Inflect carries the requirement identifiers and short titles and describes, in its own words, what each requirement asks an organisation to demonstrate.

metadata.copyright: AIUC-1 is published by the Artificial Intelligence Underwriting Company (AIUC), (c) AIUC, all rights reserved. Source: https://www.aiuc-1.com/. requirements.title: Establish input data policy
requirements.summary: Customers can read, before they send anything, what happens to the data they give the agent: whether it is used to train or tune models, how it is processed to answer a request, how long it is kept and what they can ask to have done with it. The retention periods the organisation states are carried out by an automated deletion mechanism rather than left to manual clean-up.

requirements.title: Establish output data policy
requirements.summary: Customers are told who owns what the agent produces for them, what the organisation itself may do with those outputs, how a customer opts in to or out of that use, and how an output is deleted on request; wherever an opt-out or a deletion is offered, the system actually honours it.

requirements.title: Limit AI agent data access
requirements.summary: What the agent can retrieve or read is bounded by the task in hand, the user it is acting for, its own role and the context of the session, and those bounds are enforced in retrieval and permission logic rather than in the prompt. Where proportionate, each agent holds an identity of its own, so its access can be granted, reviewed and withdrawn like anyone else's.

requirements.title: Protect IP & trade secrets
requirements.summary: The organisation's own confidential information and intellectual property do not leave through the agent. Staff are told what may not be entered into or released by AI systems, the protection model providers give submitted material is known, and, where proportionate, outputs are screened for proprietary content and suspected disclosures are reviewed.

requirements.title: Prevent cross-customer data exposure
requirements.summary: Data belonging to one customer cannot surface in another customer's session, retrieval results, fine-tuning or outputs. Separation is enforced by tenant identifiers in code and storage, and any pooling of data across customers rests on consent recorded in the customer's terms and on de-identification strong enough to resist reversal.

requirements.title: Prevent PII leakage
requirements.summary: Personal data is detected and filtered in what the agent receives, in what it returns and in the logs it leaves behind, so that personal identifiers do not reach a person, a log or a downstream system that should not hold them. Detection can be extended by routing output through an existing data-loss-prevention service.

requirements.title: Prevent IP violations
requirements.summary: What the agent produces does not infringe copyright, trademarks or other rights belonging to third parties. The organisation knows what indemnity or protection its model providers give, screens outputs for protected material where the use case warrants it, and warns users before operations that carry infringement risk. Applies to externally facing agents.

requirements.title: Prevent leakage of credentials and secrets
requirements.summary: Secrets — API keys, tokens, passwords, private keys — are caught when a user pastes one in, kept out of code the agent writes, held in a secret manager when a user hands the agent a credential to use, and redacted from logs and stored artefacts. Applies to agents that generate code.

requirements.title: Third-party testing for data & privacy risk
requirements.summary: An independent evaluator with the relevant expertise tests the system every quarter for data and privacy failures — infringing outputs, personal data and credentials leaking, business data and system instructions surfacing — scoped against the organisation's risk taxonomy, with each finding tracked to a fix and a retest.

requirements.title: Third-party testing for security risk
requirements.summary: An independent evaluator tests the system every quarter for security failures — actions, transactions, messages and data transfers the agent was never authorised to make, outputs carrying unsafe links or code, and actions that install insecure code or execute destructively — driven by attack techniques such as prompt injection and jailbreaking, with the scope drawn from the organisation's risk taxonomy.

requirements.title: Detect adversarial input
requirements.summary: Prompt-injection attempts and other adversarial input are detected while the system runs, raise an alert that somebody acts on, and are handled as incidents with a record of what happened. The detection rules are revisited every quarter in the light of the attacks actually seen. Optional under AIUC-1.

requirements.title: Manage public release of technical details
requirements.summary: What the organisation says in public about its AI systems — models, architecture, guardrails, suppliers, security posture — passes a defined approval before release, so that marketing copy, documentation and conference talks do not hand an attacker a map of the system. Optional under AIUC-1.

requirements.title: Prevent AI endpoint scraping
requirements.summary: Externally reachable AI endpoints are protected against probing, bulk extraction and model theft: per-caller rate limits and quotas, detection of anomalous usage, an external penetration test aimed at the endpoints, and a tracked path to remediation for every weakness that test finds.

requirements.title: Implement real-time input filtering
requirements.summary: Input passes through an automated moderation layer before the model acts on it, with block, warn or modify actions and confidence thresholds the organisation chose deliberately. Where proportionate, users are told when an input is blocked, flagged input is logged with privacy in mind, and the filter's error rates are measured. Optional under AIUC-1, and applies to agents that generate text, speech or images.

requirements.title: Prevent unauthorized AI agent actions
requirements.summary: An agent can act only within its intended scope and the privileges it was granted: technical controls restrict its reach into backend services and APIs, the security-relevant actions it takes are monitored and alert on misuse, and, where proportionate, its execution is contained in a sandbox. Applies to agents that take actions.

requirements.title: Enforce user access privileges to AI systems
requirements.summary: People's access to the AI system — its configuration, prompts, models, data and administrative functions — follows role- or attribute-based rules derived from policy, and that access is reviewed every quarter with each change and its justification recorded.

requirements.title: Protect AI system deployment environment
requirements.summary: The environment the AI system runs in authenticates every caller of its APIs and agent interfaces and encrypts their traffic in transit; where proportionate it also verifies model artefacts before loading them, protects the integrity of messages exchanged with agents, and hardens the hosts and containers that serve models.

requirements.title: Limit output over-exposure
requirements.summary: Output is capped in volume and, where precision would leak information, in fidelity — token and result limits, rounding or banding of sensitive figures — so that repeated querying cannot reconstruct the data or the model behind it, and users are told when an answer has been truncated or coarsened. Applies to agents that generate text, speech or images.

requirements.title: Promote secure patterns in generated code
requirements.summary: Code the agent writes defaults to secure patterns for the common vulnerability classes, for authentication and authorisation and for the choice of dependencies, and — where proportionate — for sessions and cookies, input validation, error handling and logging. Applies to agents that generate code.

requirements.title: Define AI risk taxonomy
requirements.summary: The organisation keeps its own taxonomy of AI risk, built from what its systems can do and where they are deployed, with severity levels and concrete examples for every category, and reviews it at least once a year. Testing, guardrails, monitoring and failure plans elsewhere in the standard are scoped against this taxonomy.

requirements.title: Conduct pre-deployment testing
requirements.summary: Before a change that needs formal approval reaches users, it is tested across the categories of the risk taxonomy; the issues found are rated and either fixed or accepted by a recorded decision, and release is approved on the strength of the results. Where proportionate the tests run as a gate in the delivery pipeline, artefacts and dependencies are scanned for vulnerabilities, and a changed open-weight model is regression-tested before it ships.

requirements.title: Prevent harmful outputs
requirements.summary: Output that could hurt a user — distressing or hostile replies, dangerous guidance, offensive material, biased treatment, deception — is detected and blocked or reshaped by filters and guardrails; where proportionate, the organisation also measures how well those controls perform. Applies to agents that generate text, speech or images.

requirements.title: Prevent out-of-scope outputs
requirements.summary: The agent declines subjects outside the purpose it was deployed for — a political opinion or medical guidance from an agent built for something else — through blocking rules or defensive prompting; attempts to push it out of scope are logged and used to adjust its boundaries, and users are told what it is for. Applies to agents that generate text or speech.

requirements.title: Prevent agent-specific high risk outputs
requirements.summary: Beyond the generic categories of harm, the organisation names in its risk taxonomy the high-risk outputs particular to this agent and its domain, and maps each one to detection logic and a defined response — block, modify, or hand to a person.

requirements.title: Prevent output vulnerabilities
requirements.summary: Output that a person or a system will render, run or follow is sanitised so it cannot carry script, shell or link injection into its destination, and content that came from an untrusted source is marked as such wherever it is shown. Applies to agents that generate code, text or speech.

requirements.title: Flag high risk outputs for human review
requirements.summary: The organisation defines which outputs are risky enough to need a person's review, detects them as they occur, and routes them to a reviewer through a defined workflow before they take effect or reach the user. Optional under AIUC-1.

requirements.title: Monitor AI risk categories
requirements.summary: Production output is sampled and tracked against each category of the risk taxonomy, so that a rising failure rate or a new kind of failure is noticed, recorded and fed back into the taxonomy and its controls; where the organisation runs security operations, the monitoring data reaches them. Optional under AIUC-1.

requirements.title: Enable real-time feedback and intervention
requirements.summary: Users can stop, pause or redirect the agent while it works and report a problem with what it produced; those controls are accessible, and the feedback and interventions they generate are reviewed and acted on. Optional under AIUC-1.

requirements.title: Third-party testing for safety risk
requirements.summary: An independent evaluator tests the system every quarter for safety failures — content that risks physical or emotional harm, inappropriate, biased or out-of-scope output, advice in high-risk domains such as medicine, law and finance, and the risks the organisation defined for itself — against its risk taxonomy, with each finding tracked to a fix and a retest.

requirements.title: Prevent hallucinated outputs
requirements.summary: Output is checked against the sources it claims to rest on, users are shown the citations behind an answer, and — where proportionate — the agent signals its own uncertainty, so that a fabricated statement is caught, or at least visible, rather than presented as fact. Applies to agents that generate text, speech or code.

requirements.title: Restrict unsafe tool calls
requirements.summary: Every tool or function call is checked before it runs: the tool is on an allowlist, its parameters are validated, the request is authorised, use stays inside call-rate limits and caps on value, sensitive or irreversible operations wait for a person's approval, and each call is logged with where it came from. Applies to agents that take actions.

requirements.title: Third-party testing for reliability risk
requirements.summary: An independent evaluator tests the system every quarter for reliability failures — generated or stated content that is wrong, fabricated or falsely confident, and tool calls that are mistaken, unprompted or left incomplete — scoped against the organisation's risk taxonomy, with each finding tracked to a fix and a retest.

requirements.title: AI failure plan for security breaches
requirements.summary: A written plan covers a privacy or security breach involving the AI system: who leads the response, who must be told and by when, how the system is contained and repaired, and which outside parties — legal counsel, communications, insurers, forensic support — are brought in.

requirements.title: AI failure plan for harmful outputs
requirements.summary: A written plan covers an output that does a customer significant harm: who owns the response, how the output is stopped and the customer put right, and which outside parties are engaged, with the kinds of harm it covers tied back to the risk taxonomy. Applies to externally facing agents.

requirements.title: AI failure plan for hallucinations
requirements.summary: A written plan covers a fabricated or incorrect output that costs a customer substantial money: who owns the response, how the error is traced and corrected, how affected customers are found and compensated, and which outside parties are engaged. Applies to externally facing agents.

requirements.title: Assign accountability
requirements.summary: The organisation states which changes to an AI system, anywhere from development to deployment, need formal review or approval, names an accountable lead for each kind, and keeps the approval and its supporting evidence for every such change; where proportionate, AI components are signed and the signature is checked in the delivery pipeline.

requirements.title: Document data storage security
requirements.summary: How the AI system's data is stored — where it is hosted, how it is encrypted and who can read it — is written down for each store and justified against how sensitive the data is, the regulations that apply to it and the operational need for it.

requirements.title: Conduct vendor and model due diligence
requirements.summary: Foundation-model and other upstream AI providers are assessed before use, and again on a cycle, for how they handle data and personal information, their security and their compliance, with the decision to approve them recorded; where an open-weight model is used, its source, integrity and licence are verified before it is deployed.

requirements.title: Review internal processes
requirements.summary: The key processes behind the AI system are reviewed every quarter, with each review, the decisions it took and their approval recorded, and with feedback from outside the organisation — security advisories, customer reports, researchers — weighed as part of it.

requirements.title: Monitor third-party access
requirements.summary: Connections that third parties make to the AI system — API sessions, integrations, data access — are logged in enough detail to reconstruct who reached what and when, and, where proportionate, anomalous third-party access raises an alert.

requirements.title: Establish AI acceptable use policy
requirements.summary: An acceptable use policy states what users may and may not do with the AI system; breaches of it are detected in use, the user is told when they have crossed the line, and, where the risk warrants it, further guardrails enforce it.

requirements.title: Record processing locations
requirements.summary: The organisation knows and writes down where the AI system's data is processed — its own cloud regions and inference locations and those of each AI sub-processor — and, where data crosses a border, the transfer mechanism that makes that lawful.

requirements.title: Document regulatory compliance
requirements.summary: The AI laws, regulations and standards that apply to the system are identified, together with the data protections each one requires and the organisation's approach to meeting it, and that register is reviewed at least every six months as the law moves.

requirements.title: Implement quality management system
requirements.summary: A quality management system scaled to the size of the organisation governs its AI systems: quality objectives and metrics, an approach to risk, change management, and issue tracking through to corrective action, with procedures for data management and for communicating with stakeholders where proportionate. Optional under AIUC-1.

requirements.title: Log AI system activity
requirements.summary: The AI system's processes, actions and outputs are logged, wherever the law and the customer's terms allow it, in enough detail to investigate an incident, support an audit and explain why the system behaved as it did. The logs are retained, access-controlled and sanitised, an agent's execution can be attributed to it, and log integrity is protected where proportionate.

requirements.title: Implement AI disclosure mechanisms
requirements.summary: Users are told plainly, in every modality the system works in — text, voice, generated media, automated actions — that they are dealing with an AI system rather than a person.

requirements.title: Document system transparency policy
requirements.summary: The organisation keeps a transparency policy and current transparency documentation for each major system (model cards, datasheets, AI bills of materials), says when and with whom that material is shared, and documents how security responsibilities divide between the platform and whoever deploys it. Optional under AIUC-1.

requirements.title: Third-party testing for accountability risk
requirements.summary: An independent evaluator tests the system every quarter for accountability failures — above all an agent that conceals, denies or can be talked out of disclosing that it is an AI — against the organisation's risk taxonomy, with each finding tracked to a fix and a retest.

requirements.title: Prevent AI cyber misuse
requirements.summary: The organisation knows what its foundation models can do to assist a cyber attack, from the providers' own assessments, and puts or documents guardrails that stop the agent being used to write malicious code or to plan and carry out exploitation; a model it has modified is reassessed rather than assumed to keep the provider's results. Applies to agents that generate text, speech or code, or that take actions.

requirements.title: Prevent catastrophic misuse
requirements.summary: The organisation knows what each foundation model it uses can contribute to chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear harm, from the providers' own assessments, and puts or documents guardrails against that use, monitoring for it where proportionate. Applies to agents that generate text, speech or images.

templates.title: Customer input data use, retention and rights published and enforced
templates.description: The terms a customer accepts before first use say how data sent to the agent is used to answer requests and whether it trains any model, how long each kind of input is kept and what the customer may ask for — and automated deletion carries out the retention those terms state.
templates.defaultOwnerHint: Data Protection Officer / Platform Engineering Lead
templates.objective: To ensure every customer can learn before use how their agent inputs are used, kept and deleted, and that the retention the organisation states is the retention its systems apply.
templates.successCriteria:
The accepted terms state whether agent inputs train or tune any model, how they are used to serve a request, and a retention period for each kind of input.
Every store holding agent inputs, including provider-held copies, logs and evaluation sets, is inventoried with the period it should apply.
Automated deletion is configured on each inventoried store and its run log shows inputs removed at the stated period.
Customer requests to opt out of training use, export or delete their inputs follow a documented route and are completed within the period the terms commit to.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the terms of service, privacy notice and data processing agreement customers accept before using the agent, with effective dates.
Obtain the inventory of stores holding agent inputs and the retention period assigned to each.
Obtain the deletion job, lifecycle rule or time-to-live configuration for each store, and its run logs for the period.
Obtain the register of customer data-rights requests about agent inputs received in the period.

Analysis:
Read the terms for the four points they must settle — training use, use to serve a request, retention, customer rights — and note any left unstated or ambiguous.
Trace each inventoried store to a deletion mechanism and compare its configured period with the period the terms state.
Query a sample of each store for inputs older than their retention period and confirm none remain.
Compare data-flow and architecture records with the inventory to find input stores it omits.
Sample the request register and compare completion dates with the period the terms commit to.

Output:
A statement of which of the four points the published terms settle and which they leave open.
A store-by-store table of stated against applied retention, naming every store without automated deletion.
A list of requests completed late or not at all, and of input stores found outside the inventory.

title.en: Inventory every store that holds data customers send to the agent

description.en: Agent inputs travel further than the conversation window: chat history, uploaded files, retrieval caches, application and model-provider logs, and copies kept for evaluation or fine-tuning. List each store, the kind of input it holds, who operates it — including model providers and other sub-processors — and the retention period it is meant to apply. Attach the inventory with its date and the name of whoever compiled it.

evidenceHint.en: Inventory of input stores, one row per store, naming the input it holds, its operator and its intended retention period

text.en: List the stores your own systems use for conversation history, uploads and caches.
Add the copies kept by model providers and other sub-processors, taken from their terms.
Include logs, analytics exports and evaluation or fine-tuning sets that carry inputs.
Note against each store the kind of input it holds and the period it should keep it.
Date the inventory and name the person who compiled it.

title.en: Publish how customer inputs are used, kept and deleted in the terms customers accept

description.en: Write the input data terms into the terms of service, privacy notice or data processing agreement a customer accepts before first use. They must say whether inputs train or tune any model and whether a customer can refuse, how inputs are processed to answer a request, the retention period for each kind of input in the inventory, and the rights a customer holds over them. Attach the published text with its effective date.

evidenceHint.en: Published terms, privacy notice or DPA section covering training use, request processing, retention periods and customer rights for agent inputs, with its effective date

text.en: State plainly whether inputs train or tune any model and whether customers can refuse.
Describe how inputs are processed to answer a request, naming any sub-processor involved.
Give the retention period for each kind of input named in the store inventory.
List the rights customers hold over their inputs and how each one is exercised.
Publish the text where customers accept it before first use and note the effective date.

title.en: Configure automated deletion for each input store at its stated retention period

description.en: For every store in the inventory, set up the mechanism that removes inputs once their period ends — a scheduled deletion job, a storage lifecycle rule or a database time-to-live — and have it log what it removes on each run. Where a provider holds the copy, capture the account setting or contract term that bounds how long it is kept. Attach the configuration for each store.

evidenceHint.en: Deletion job, lifecycle rule or time-to-live configuration for each input store, showing the configured period, plus the provider setting or clause for provider-held copies

text.en: Pick the deletion mechanism each store supports: scheduled job, lifecycle rule or time-to-live.
Set each configured period to the retention period the published terms state.
Have each mechanism log the count or identifiers of what it deletes on every run.
Capture the provider setting or contract clause that limits copies held by sub-processors.
File each configuration beside the inventory row it implements.

title.en: Complete customer requests to opt out of, export or delete their agent inputs

description.en: Take every request a customer makes about their inputs — refusing training use, obtaining a copy, having them deleted — through a documented procedure that reaches each store in the inventory, provider-held copies included, and log the date it arrived and the date it was finished. Attach the request register for the period.

evidenceHint.en: Register of data-rights requests about agent inputs, giving receipt date, stores actioned and completion date for each

text.en: Log each request on arrival with the customer, the right exercised and the date.
Carry out the request in every store the inventory lists, provider-held copies included.
Enter the completion date and the stores actioned against the request.
Confirm completion to the customer and file that confirmation with the request.

title.en: Sample input stores for data held past its stated retention period

description.en: Once a year, query each inventoried store for inputs older than its retention period, check the deletion logs for runs that were missed, and compare the published terms against the inventory for any store or kind of input they fail to cover. Attach the sample results, with every discrepancy, the fix agreed and its owner.

evidenceHint.en: Per-store retention sample results and deletion-log check, with each discrepancy, its agreed fix and its owner

text.en: Query each inventoried store for inputs older than its stated retention period.
Check the deletion logs for gaps where a mechanism failed to run in the period.
Compare the published terms with the inventory for stores or input types they omit.
Search the period's architecture changes for new stores holding inputs not yet listed.
Enter each discrepancy with its agreed fix, owner and target date.

templates.title: Ownership, reuse and deletion of agent outputs settled in customer terms and honoured
templates.description: Customer-facing terms settle who owns what the agent generates and how that differs by kind of output, what the organisation may itself do with outputs, and how a customer opts in to or out of that use or has an output deleted. Where an opt-out or a deletion is offered, a stored consent choice and a deletion workflow make the platform act on it.
templates.defaultOwnerHint: Legal Counsel / Data Protection Officer / Platform Engineering Lead
templates.objective: To give customers a clear statement of who owns agent outputs and how the organisation may reuse or delete them, and to make every opt-out and deletion it offers take effect.
templates.successCriteria:
The customer terms state who owns agent outputs as distinct from inputs, the uses a customer may make of them and any restriction, by kind of output.
The terms state each use the organisation makes of outputs beyond serving the customer and how long each kind of output is kept.
Every choice the terms offer over outputs, whether opting in, opting out or deletion, has a documented route, and a customer can withdraw a permission given earlier.
Each location that stores or reuses outputs reads the customer's consent choice, and opted-out or deleted outputs are absent from it.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the customer agreement and any data or AI terms attached to it as in force during the period, with effective dates.
Obtain the catalogue of agent output types and of every location where outputs are stored or reused.
Obtain the consent-record and deletion-workflow configuration, with their execution logs for the period.
Obtain the register of customer opt-in, opt-out, withdrawal and output-deletion requests received in the period.

Analysis:
Read the terms for ownership by output type, permitted customer use, the organisation's own reuse, output retention and each choice offered, and note any point left unstated or contradictory.
Trace each catalogued reuse location to the point where it reads the consent record and name any location that ignores it.
Select a sample of opted-out customers and query each reuse location, training and evaluation sets first, for their outputs.
Select a sample of completed deletion requests and query every catalogued location for the outputs removed.
Compare the register's completion dates with the period the terms commit to.

Output:
A statement of which ownership, use and choice points the terms settle and which they leave open.
A location-by-location table showing whether each honours opt-out and deletion.
A list of outputs found after an opt-out or deletion, and of requests completed late or not at all.

title.en: Catalogue each kind of agent output and every place its copies are kept or reused

description.en: Ownership clauses and opt-outs can only be written, and honoured, against a known population. List the kinds of output the agent produces — generated text, files, code, summaries, records of actions it took — and every place copies of them go: conversation history, output caches, analytics exports, evaluation or fine-tuning sets, and copies held by model providers or other sub-processors. Mark each place that reuses outputs for anything beyond answering the customer. Attach the dated catalogue.

evidenceHint.en: Dated catalogue of agent output types and of each location holding or reusing them, marking locations that reuse outputs beyond serving the customer

text.en: List the output types the agent returns, from generated text and files to records of actions.
Trace where each output type is written: history, caches, exports and provider-side copies.
Add the analytics, evaluation and fine-tuning sets that are built from stored outputs.
Flag every location that reuses outputs for a purpose other than answering the customer.
Date the catalogue and name the engineer who compiled it.

title.en: Write output ownership and permitted-use clauses into the customer agreement

description.en: Draft the clauses that say who owns agent outputs as distinct from the inputs a customer supplies, whether the customer may use outputs commercially, modify them and share them, and any restriction that applies — stating plainly where ownership or permitted use differs between the output types in the catalogue. Add each use the organisation itself makes of outputs. Place the clauses in the agreement customers accept. Attach the clauses as published, with their effective date.

evidenceHint.en: Published agreement section stating output ownership by output type, permitted customer uses, restrictions and the organisation's own uses, with effective date

text.en: State who owns outputs and how that differs from ownership of the customer's inputs.
Set out the uses customers may make of outputs, including commercial use and onward sharing.
Name each restriction on outputs and the output types it covers.
Describe each use the organisation makes of outputs, such as storage, quality review or training.
Publish the clauses in the agreement customers accept and note the effective date.

title.en: Set out the choices customers hold over agent outputs: opting in, opting out and deletion

description.en: In the customer terms or privacy notice, explain each choice a customer has over outputs: whether each reuse is off until they opt in or on until they opt out, how to change or withdraw a permission already given, how to ask for outputs to be deleted, and how long each kind of output is kept and how it is handled until then. Name the route through which each choice is exercised. Attach the published text with its effective date.

evidenceHint.en: Published text describing output opt-in or opt-out, withdrawal of permission, deletion requests and output retention periods, with effective date

text.en: State whether each reuse the catalogue marks is opt-in or opt-out.
Explain how a customer withdraws a permission they granted earlier.
Describe how to request deletion of outputs and which locations a deletion reaches.
Give the retention period that applies to each kind of output in the catalogue.
Publish the text where customers read their terms and note the effective date.

title.en: Build the consent check and deletion workflow that act on stored agent outputs

description.en: Where the terms offer an opt-out or deletion, and to the degree the deployment calls for automated enforcement, hold each customer's choice in one consent record and have every reuse location in the catalogue read it before an output is kept or reused — through a feature flag or a pipeline filter, for example. Build a deletion workflow that removes a customer's outputs from every catalogued location and logs each run with a timestamp. Attach the configuration and a sample of its logs.

evidenceHint.en: Consent-record and deletion-workflow configuration showing each reuse location reading the customer's choice, with timestamped execution logs

text.en: Store each customer's output choice in a single consent record keyed to the customer.
Make each catalogued reuse location check that record before keeping or reusing an output.
Exclude opted-out customers' outputs when evaluation and training sets are built.
Script a deletion run that reaches every catalogued location, provider-held copies included.
Log each consent check and deletion run with a timestamp and the customer affected.

title.en: Resolve each customer opt-out and output-deletion request in every catalogued location

description.en: Take every request about outputs — opting in, opting out, withdrawing a permission, deleting outputs — through the published route: open a register entry, change the consent record or start the deletion workflow, confirm from the workflow log that each catalogued location was reached, provider-held copies included, and tell the customer when it is done. Engineering runs the workflow; the register stays with the privacy owner. Attach the request register for the period.

evidenceHint.en: Register of output opt-in, opt-out, withdrawal and deletion requests with receipt date, locations actioned, completion date and customer confirmation

text.en: Open a register entry per request naming the customer, the choice and the arrival date.
Change the consent record or start the deletion workflow for that customer.
Check the workflow log shows every catalogued location reached, provider copies included.
Enter the completion date and send the customer confirmation of the outcome.

title.en: Sample opted-out and deleted customers for outputs still stored or reused

description.en: Once a year, pick a sample of customers who opted out and of completed deletion requests, and query each catalogued location — evaluation and training sets especially — for outputs that should no longer be there. Compare current architecture records with the catalogue for new reuse locations, and the published terms with the catalogue for output types they omit. Attach the sample results with each discrepancy, its agreed fix and its owner.

evidenceHint.en: Sample results per reuse location for opted-out and deleted customers, with each residual output or gap, its agreed fix and its owner

text.en: Draw a sample of opted-out customers and of deletion requests closed in the period.
Query each catalogued location for outputs belonging to the sampled customers.
Check training and evaluation set manifests for outputs from opted-out customers.
Compare current architecture records with the catalogue for unlisted reuse locations.
Enter each residual output or gap with its agreed fix, owner and target date.

templates.title: Agent retrieval bounded by the task, the requesting user's role and the session
templates.description: Limits on what an agent can read or retrieve, enforced in retrieval filters and permission checks rather than in the prompt: results are cut to the task in hand, the role of the user the agent acts for and the current session, and retrieved data does not outlive the session that needed it. Where proportionate, each agent holds an identity of its own whose data scopes are granted and withdrawn like a person's.
templates.defaultOwnerHint: AI Platform Lead / Data Protection Officer
templates.objective: To ensure an agent can read only the data its current task, the user it acts for and its session warrant, with those limits enforced in code that no prompt can talk its way around.
templates.successCriteria:
Every data source an agent reads is mapped to the tasks needing it, the user roles entitled to its records and any session limit.
Retrieval code applies the acting user's permissions and the task's scope to results before any of them enter the model context.
Retrieval caches and scratch storage are keyed to one session and cleared at its end, and any long-term memory is confined to its own user.
Where agents hold identities, each has unique credentials and its own task's scopes, never a parent agent's by default.
Test requests outside the user's role, the task or the session are refused with an explicit error.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the data-source scope map for each agent in production, with its date.
Obtain the retrieval filter and permission-check code or configuration for each source, and the session-scoping settings for caches and memory.
Obtain the agent identity register and each identity's data scopes, where agents hold identities of their own.
Obtain the change records for agents and data sources connected or withdrawn during the period.

Analysis:
Trace each source in the scope map to the filter or check that enforces its scope, and note any source bounded only by prompt instructions.
Run a sample of retrieval requests as test users of differing roles and confirm results stay within each user's permissions.
Open two sessions for one test user and confirm session-scoped data retrieved in the first cannot be reached from the second.
Compare each agent identity's granted scopes with the scope map and check sub-agents for scopes beyond their own task.
Sample connections made in the period and confirm each had its scope-map row and filter in place before go-live.

Output:
A source-by-source table of intended against enforced scope, naming every source bounded only by the prompt.
A list of test requests that returned data outside the user's role, the task or the session.
A list of agent identities holding scopes the map does not justify, and of sources connected without a scope set.

title.en: Map each agent's data sources to the task, user role and session scope it may read

description.en: For every agent in production, list the knowledge bases, vector indexes, databases, file stores and APIs it retrieves from. Against each source, write down which tasks need it, which user roles may see its records through the agent, and whether reads must stay within the current session or workflow stage. Mark any source the agent can reach that no current task needs. Attach the scope map with its date and the name of whoever compiled it.

evidenceHint.en: Data-source scope map per agent, one row per source, giving the tasks that need it, the user roles entitled to its records and its session or stage limit

text.en: List every index, database, file store and API each production agent retrieves from.
Name the tasks or workflow stages that need each source, and those that do not.
Write the user roles whose records the agent may return from each source.
Mark the sources whose reads must stay within one session or workflow stage.
Flag any reachable source that no current task needs, so it can be disconnected.

title.en: Enforce the requesting user's record permissions inside the agent's retrieval function

description.en: Apply the scope map in the code that fetches data, not in the system prompt. Pass the identity and role of the user the agent acts for into every retrieval call, filter documents and rows by that user's permissions and by the current task before results enter the model context, and have a query outside those bounds return an explicit error rather than a quietly empty answer. Attach the filter code or configuration for each source and a sample refusal.

evidenceHint.en: Retrieval filter code or configuration per source, showing the acting user's identity, role and task applied before results enter the model context, with a sample refusal

text.en: Pass the acting user's identity and role into every retrieval call the agent makes.
Filter documents and rows by that user's permissions before results reach the model.
Narrow results further to the sources and fields the current task needs.
Return an explicit error for a query outside the user's or the task's scope.
Replace scope rules that live only in the system prompt with the equivalent code check.

title.en: Bind retrieved data, caches and agent memory to a single session and workflow stage

description.en: Stop data persisting beyond the context that justified reading it. Key retrieval caches, scratch storage and conversation memory to the session identifier rather than to the user alone, clear them when the session ends, and gate reads of stage-specific sources on the workflow stage the task has reached. Where long-term memory is a product feature, confine it to the user it was gathered from. Attach the session-scoping configuration and the settings of the clean-up job.

evidenceHint.en: Session-scoping configuration keying caches and memory to the session identifier, the end-of-session clean-up settings and the stage gates on stage-specific sources

text.en: Key retrieval caches and scratch storage to the session identifier, not the user alone.
Clear session-keyed data when the session ends or times out.
Gate reads of stage-specific sources on the workflow stage the task has reached.
Confine any long-term memory feature to the user it was gathered from.

title.en: Issue each agent a unique identity carrying its own data-read scopes

description.en: Where proportionate, for example where several agents or sub-agents share one platform, give every agent its own verifiable identity, such as a workload identity or a federated OIDC client, in place of a shared service account. Grant it only the scopes its row in the scope map allows, mapped to enterprise roles; issue short-lived credentials for single subtasks where the platform supports it; and do not let a sub-agent take on its orchestrator's wider scopes by default. Attach the identity register with each identity's scopes.

evidenceHint.en: Agent identity register naming each agent's unique identity, its data scopes mapped to enterprise roles, its credential lifetime and any parent agent it runs under

text.en: Replace shared service accounts with one identity per agent or sub-agent.
Map each identity's data scopes to the enterprise roles they correspond to.
Issue credentials scoped to a single subtask, with a short lifetime, where the platform allows.
Grant each sub-agent its own task's scopes rather than its orchestrator's.
Flag scope combinations across identities that would break segregation of duties.

title.en: Set the read scope for each new agent or data source before it is connected

description.en: Whenever an agent is added, or a new data source is connected to one, add its row to the scope map, configure the matching retrieval filter and session limits and, where agents hold identities, grant the scopes to that identity, all before the connection goes live. Withdraw the scopes and filters the same way when an agent is retired or a source is disconnected. Attach the change record for each connection or withdrawal made in the period.

evidenceHint.en: Change records for agents and data sources connected or withdrawn in the period, each showing the scope-map row and retrieval filter configured before go-live

text.en: Add the new agent or source to the scope map with its task, role and session limits.
Configure the retrieval filter and session limits before the connection is enabled.
Grant the matching scopes to the agent's identity where agents hold their own.
Withdraw scopes and filters when an agent is retired or a source is disconnected.
Link each change record to the scope-map row it created or removed.

title.en: Test whether the agent returns records outside the user's role, task or session

description.en: Once a year, run retrieval tests against each production agent: ask, as a lower-privileged test user, for records that user should not see; ask for data unrelated to the active task; and ask a fresh session for session-scoped data retrieved in an earlier one. Compare what comes back with the scope map, and compare agent identities' granted scopes with it too. Attach the test log with every leak found, the fix agreed and its owner.

evidenceHint.en: Retrieval test log per agent showing role, task and cross-session test queries, their results against the scope map, and each leak with its fix and owner

text.en: Create test users at differing roles and query each agent for records above their role.
Ask for data unrelated to the active task and note what the agent returns.
Query a new session for session-scoped data retrieved in an earlier one.
Compare the scopes granted to agent identities against the scope map.
Log each leak with the agreed fix, its owner and a target date.

templates.title: The organisation's own trade secrets and confidential data kept from leaking through AI
templates.description: Staff are told which of the organisation's own confidential information and intellectual property — trade secrets, unreleased code, internal plans — must never go into AI tools, and the confidentiality each model provider gives submitted material is known and held on file. Where proportionate, agent outputs are screened for proprietary markers and suspected disclosures go to a person for review.
templates.defaultOwnerHint: Information Security Lead / Legal Counsel
templates.objective: To keep the organisation's own trade secrets and confidential information from leaving through AI tools and agents, whether by what staff submit or by what an agent returns.
templates.successCriteria:
A classification states which kinds of company confidential information and IP staff may not enter into AI tools, and which approved tools may receive each kind.
Staff who use AI tools have received guidance setting out those rules, and the organisation can show who received it and when.
Each model provider receiving staff or agent submissions has its retention and training-use commitments on file, with the account settings applying them.
Where screening is proportionate, outputs carrying proprietary labels, codenames or confidential-source content are blocked or flagged, and every flag has a review outcome.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the classification of company information by permitted AI use, with its date.
Obtain the staff guidance or training material on AI and confidential information, and the record of who received it in the period.
Obtain each model provider's contract, data processing terms or AI addendum covering retention and training use of submitted material, and screenshots of the account settings applied.
Obtain the output-screening configuration, its list of proprietary markers, and the register of flagged outputs reviewed in the period.

Analysis:
Compare the AI tools in use, taken from procurement and single sign-on records, with the tools the classification approves.
Select a sample of staff who used AI tools in the period and confirm each received the guidance.
Compare each provider's stated retention and training commitments with the account settings actually enabled.
Submit test requests for material the classification protects and confirm the screen blocks or flags each one.
Sample the flagged-output register and confirm each entry has a reviewer, a decision and, where a disclosure was confirmed, a follow-up action.

Output:
A list of AI tools in use that the classification does not cover, and of sampled staff without the guidance.
A provider-by-provider table of committed against configured retention and training use.
The screening test results, and the flagged outputs left without a recorded review.

title.en: Classify which company confidential information may never be entered into AI tools

description.en: Set out the categories of the organisation's own confidential information and intellectual property that matter for AI use — trade secrets, unreleased source code, product roadmaps, financial forecasts, deal material, information held under a non-disclosure agreement — and decide for each whether it may go to any approved AI tool, only to named tools under enterprise terms, or to none. Attach the dated classification.

evidenceHint.en: Classification of company confidential information by permitted AI use, naming the approved tools for each category, with its date and compiler

text.en: List the categories of confidential information and IP the organisation holds, with an example of each.
Name the AI tools staff can reach, separating approved enterprise tools from public ones.
Mark each category as permitted, permitted only in named tools, or prohibited.
Check each marking with the team that owns that category of information.
Date the classification and name the person who compiled it.

title.en: Train staff on the confidential information they must not paste into AI tools

description.en: Turn the classification into guidance staff can apply: what must never be pasted, uploaded or dictated into an AI tool, which approved tools may take which material, and who to tell after a mistaken submission. Legal/DPO owns the content; deliver it through onboarding and the training staff take before using AI tools, and keep a distribution record. Attach the guidance and the record of who received it in the period.

evidenceHint.en: Staff guidance or training material on AI use and company confidential information, with the distribution or completion record for the period

text.en: Write the prohibited and permitted categories in plain terms with one worked example each.
Name the approved AI tools and the material each one may receive.
Give the contact and route for reporting a mistaken submission of confidential material.
Add the guidance to onboarding and to the training staff take before using AI tools.
Export the list of staff who received or completed it, with dates.

title.en: Obtain the retention and no-training commitments providers give for company material staff submit

description.en: Where proportionate to the sensitivity of what is sent, obtain the clauses governing what a foundation model provider does with material from staff tools or the agent: whether submissions are retained and for how long, whether they train any model, who at the provider may see them, and whether a zero-retention or enhanced-privacy tier exists. Confirm that tier is switched on for the organisation's accounts and steer sensitive use cases to providers offering it. Attach the provider commitments register.

evidenceHint.en: Register of model providers giving retention period, training use and confidentiality clauses for submitted material, with contract reference and the account setting applied

text.en: List every model provider that receives material from staff tools or the agent.
Extract each provider's clauses on retention, training use and staff access to submissions.
Note whether a zero-retention or enhanced-privacy tier exists and its contract reference.
Capture a screenshot of the account setting that applies the commitment.
Flag providers that cannot commit to no training use for material limited to named tools.

title.en: Configure output screening for proprietary labels, codenames and confidential-source content

description.en: Where the agent can reach company material its recipients should not receive, and screening is proportionate to that exposure, add a check on outputs before delivery. Label proprietary files and repositories, write rules for internal classification markers, project codenames and the terms the classification protects, and tag responses that drew on sources labelled confidential. Decide per rule whether to block, redact or flag for review. Attach the rule set and its configuration.

evidenceHint.en: Output-screening configuration and rule list for proprietary markers, showing the action each rule takes, and the labels applied to confidential sources

text.en: Apply confidentiality labels to the repositories and document stores the agent can read.
Write rules for classification markers, project codenames and terms the classification lists.
Tag responses whose retrieved context came from a source labelled confidential.
Set each rule to block, redact or flag, and route flags to the review queue.
Version the rule set and store its configuration with the change reference.

title.en: Triage outputs flagged as possibly disclosing company trade secrets or confidential plans

description.en: Where screening is in place, work the queue it feeds: for each flagged output a reviewer decides whether company confidential information actually left, who received it, and what follows — correcting or withdrawing the response, informing the information owner, tightening a rule, or closing it as a false positive. Attach the flagged-output register for the period with each decision.

evidenceHint.en: Flagged-output register for the period, giving each output's trigger, reviewer, decision and follow-up action

text.en: Open each flagged output with the context and source the screen captured.
Decide whether confidential company information reached someone not entitled to it.
Tell the information owner of every confirmed disclosure and agree the follow-up.
Mark false positives and pass recurring ones to the rule owner for tuning.
Close each entry with the reviewer's name, date and decision.

title.en: Test the proprietary screen with requests for unreleased code and internal plans

description.en: Send the agent requests designed to draw out material the classification protects — unreleased source code, documents labelled confidential, codename projects, internal forecasts — and check each response is refused, redacted or flagged as the rules intend. Run the requests from a test account against the production configuration. Attach the test log and the list of gaps with owners.

evidenceHint.en: Test log of probing requests with the expected and observed screen action for each, and the list of gaps found with owners

text.en: Write probing requests for each protected category the screen covers.
Run them from a test account against the production agent configuration.
Compare the observed block, redaction or flag with the action each rule intends.
Enter each miss with the rule at fault, the fix agreed and its owner.

templates.title: One customer's data never surfaces in another customer's sessions, results or models
templates.description: Every store and pipeline the agent uses keeps each customer's data apart — tenant identifiers enforced in schemas, per-tenant partitions in vector indexes and caches, separate fine-tuning sets — and data is pooled across customers only where the customer's terms record consent, an opt-out is honoured, and de-identification resists reversal.
templates.defaultOwnerHint: Platform Engineering Lead / Data Protection Officer
templates.objective: To ensure data belonging to one customer cannot reach another customer through shared storage, vector indexes, caching, fine-tuning or pooled analytics.
templates.successCriteria:
Every store and pipeline holding data from more than one customer is mapped with the isolation mechanism it relies on.
Shared databases, vector indexes, caches and fine-tuning sets enforce a tenant identifier or a per-tenant partition, and a request from one tenant returns none of another tenant's records.
Any pooled use of customer data is disclosed in the terms the customer accepts, with the de-identification applied and an opt-out, and each customer's choice is registered.
Each pooled dataset is built only from customers whose registered choice permits it, after de-identification tested against reversal.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the map of stores and pipelines holding data from more than one customer, with the isolation mechanism of each.
Obtain the schemas, row-level security policies, vector-index namespace configuration and cache-key design that implement tenant separation.
Obtain the clauses of the terms of service or DPA on pooled use, and the consent and opt-out register.
Obtain the build records of each pooled dataset in the period, with the de-identification applied and its reversal test.
Obtain the results of the cross-tenant canary test.

Analysis:
Compare the map with architecture diagrams and infrastructure inventories to find shared stores it omits.
Inspect the isolation configuration of each mapped store and confirm a caller cannot omit or override the tenant identifier.
Re-run a sample of canary queries from one test tenant seeking another tenant's records.
Trace each pooled dataset to the consent register and confirm no opted-out or unconsented customer contributed.
Read the reversal test for each de-identification method and judge whether linkage with data an insider holds could re-identify a customer.

Output:
A store-by-store statement of the isolation enforced, naming any store that relies on application convention alone.
A list of canary records retrieved across tenants, and of pooled datasets holding data the register does not permit.
A judgement on the strength of each de-identification method.

title.en: Map every store and pipeline where data from different customers sits together

description.en: Trace where customer data goes once the agent receives it — relational databases, vector indexes, conversation and response caches, object storage, fine-tuning and evaluation sets, analytics warehouses and logs — and mark each as dedicated to one customer or shared. For each shared one, name the isolation mechanism it relies on, or note that it has none. Attach the map with its date.

evidenceHint.en: Map of stores and pipelines holding customer data, marking each as dedicated or shared and naming the isolation mechanism of each shared one

text.en: List the databases, vector indexes and caches the agent reads from or writes to.
Add the fine-tuning, evaluation and analytics datasets built from customer data.
Mark each store as single-customer or shared across customers.
Name the isolation mechanism each shared store relies on, or note that none exists.
Date the map and link it to the architecture diagram it was checked against.

title.en: Enforce tenant separation in shared schemas, vector indexes, caches and tuning sets

description.en: For each shared store in the map, put the separation in the storage layer rather than in calling code alone: a mandatory tenant identifier with row-level security in shared tables, a namespace or collection per tenant in the vector index, cache keys that carry the tenant, and a separate fine-tuning set and adapter per customer where models are tuned on their data. Apply tenant-specific encryption keys where the architecture uses them. Attach the configuration for each store.

evidenceHint.en: Schema and row-level security policies, vector-index namespace configuration, cache-key design and per-tenant tuning-set layout for each shared store

text.en: Make the tenant identifier mandatory in every shared table and enable row-level security.
Create a namespace or collection per tenant in the vector index and write each tenant's embeddings only there.
Include the tenant identifier in every conversation and response cache key.
Hold each customer's fine-tuning data and adapters where no other tenant's job can read them.
Export the configuration of each store and file it beside its row in the map.

title.en: Publish pooled-use terms and register each customer's consent or opt-out

description.en: Where data from several customers is combined — to train or tune a shared model, to build benchmarks, or in analytics that competitors also contribute to — say so in the terms of service or DPA before it happens: what is combined, the de-identification applied, and how a customer opts out. Where nothing is pooled, the terms say that instead. Keep a register of each customer's choice. Attach the clause and the register.

evidenceHint.en: Terms of service or DPA clause disclosing pooled use, de-identification and opt-out, with its effective date, and the register of each customer's consent or opt-out

text.en: List every current or planned use that combines data from more than one customer.
Draft the clause naming each use, the de-identification applied and the opt-out route.
Publish the clause in the terms customers accept and note the effective date.
Enter each customer's consent or opt-out in the register with the date it was given.

title.en: Implement de-identification that resists reversal before customer data is pooled

description.en: Where the deployment pools customer data, apply a privacy-enhancing technique, chosen in proportion to what is pooled, before data leaves the customer's partition: keyed tokenisation or hashing of identifiers, masking of names and account details, aggregation with differential privacy, or federated training that never centralises raw records. Test each method by trying to link its output back to a customer. Attach the method description and the reversal test.

evidenceHint.en: Description of the de-identification method for each pooled dataset, its configuration, and the reversal test with the linkage attempted and its result

text.en: Choose a de-identification method for each pooled dataset and note why it suits the data.
Hold tokenisation and hashing keys outside the pooled environment.
Attempt re-identification using auxiliary data an insider or another customer could hold.
Strengthen or replace any method the attempt reverses before the dataset is used.

title.en: Check each pooled dataset build against the customer consent register

description.en: Before any dataset combining data from several customers is built or refreshed, compare its contributing customers with the consent register as it stood on the build date, drop every customer who opted out or never consented, and confirm de-identification ran. Keep a build record listing contributors, exclusions and the de-identification run. Attach the build records for the period.

evidenceHint.en: Build record for each pooled dataset in the period, listing contributing customers, excluded customers and the de-identification run

text.en: Export the contributing customer list from the dataset build job.
Compare it with the consent register as it stood on the build date.
Remove opted-out and unconsented customers and rebuild if any were present.
Log the de-identification run identifier against the build.
Store the build record with the dataset version it describes.

title.en: Test tenant isolation by seeking one test tenant's canary records from another

description.en: Create two test tenants and seed each with distinctive canary records — documents, conversation turns, embeddings and, where tuning is per customer, tuning examples. From the first tenant, ask the agent for the second tenant's canaries through chat, retrieval, cached answers and any tuned model, and query the shared stores directly with the first tenant's credentials. Attach the test script, each attempt and its result.

evidenceHint.en: Cross-tenant test script and results, showing each canary sought, the path tried and whether any record crossed tenants

text.en: Create two test tenants and seed each with uniquely marked canary records.
Request the other tenant's canaries through chat, retrieval and cached answers.
Query each shared store directly using the first tenant's credentials.
Prompt any per-customer tuned model for the other tenant's tuning examples.
Open a defect for every canary that crosses tenants and track it to a fix.

templates.title: Personal data detected and filtered in agent prompts, responses and logs
templates.description: Personal identifiers are found and handled at each point the agent touches them: masked or blocked in prompts and responses before display, scrubbed from application logs, traces and stored transcripts before they are written, and kept out of retained outputs. Where the organisation already runs data-loss prevention, agent responses also pass through its personal data rules.
templates.defaultOwnerHint: Data Protection Officer / Platform Engineering Lead
templates.objective: To prevent personal identifiers in what the agent receives, returns or records from reaching a user, a log or a downstream system that should not hold them.
templates.successCriteria:
A defined list of personal identifiers states, for prompts, responses and logs, whether each is allowed, masked or blocked.
Prompts and responses pass through personal data detection, and responses exposing identifiers the recipient should not see are masked or blocked before display.
Application logs, traces and stored transcripts are scrubbed of personal identifiers before write, and outputs holding sensitive personal data are not retained beyond the task.
Every personal data block raised by the response filter or the DLP service in the period has a recorded disposition.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the personal identifier list with the handling set for prompts, responses and logs.
Obtain the detection and masking configuration on the prompt and response paths, and the DLP integration where one exists.
Obtain the redaction rules for each logging pipeline and transcript store, and the retention setting for outputs holding sensitive personal data.
Obtain the register of personal data block events and their dispositions for the period.

Analysis:
Pass a set of synthetic personal records covering every listed identifier through the agent and compare the observed handling on each path with the list.
Draw a random sample of log lines and stored transcripts from the period and scan them for listed identifiers.
Compare the logging pipelines and transcript stores in the architecture with those carrying redaction rules.
Sample the block events and confirm each was dispositioned, and that sources repeatedly surfacing identifiers were followed up.

Output:
A per-identifier table of intended against observed handling on each path.
The count and location of personal identifiers found in sampled logs and transcripts.
A list of pipelines or stores without redaction, and of block events left without a disposition.

title.en: Define the personal identifiers the agent must mask or block, path by path

description.en: List the kinds of personal data the deployment can meet — names, email addresses, phone numbers, national identity and account numbers, health or financial details — and decide, separately for prompts, responses and logs, whether each is allowed because the task needs it, masked, or blocked. Name the downstream systems that receive agent output and what each may hold. Attach the identifier list with its handling decisions.

evidenceHint.en: Personal identifier list giving, for prompts, responses and logs, whether each identifier is allowed, masked or blocked, plus the downstream systems receiving output

text.en: List the personal data types users submit and the agent's sources contain.
Set the handling for each type on the prompt path, the response path and in logs.
Note where a task legitimately needs an identifier and who may then see it.
Name each downstream system receiving agent output and the identifiers it may hold.
Date the list and name the person who compiled it.

title.en: Configure personal data detection on prompts and on responses before they are displayed

description.en: Put a detector — pattern rules for structured identifiers and an entity recogniser for names and addresses — on the prompt path and the response path, applying the handling the identifier list sets: mask what the model does not need, and mask or block a response that would expose an identifier its recipient should not see. Where the organisation already operates DLP and the deployment calls for it, send responses through its personal data policies as a second check. Attach the configuration and a test output.

evidenceHint.en: Detection and masking configuration for the prompt and response paths, a test output showing masking and blocking, and the DLP policy binding where used

text.en: Add pattern rules for structured identifiers such as phone, card and national ID numbers.
Add an entity recogniser for names and postal addresses in free text.
Wire each detector to the allow, mask or block action the identifier list sets.
Connect the response path to the DLP service's personal data policies where one exists.
Capture a test output showing an identifier masked and a response blocked.

title.en: Remove personal identifiers from logs, traces and transcripts before they are written

description.en: Apply the same detection at every place agent traffic is persisted — application logs, tracing spans, analytics events, stored conversation transcripts — so identifiers are replaced before the write, not cleaned up after it. Move fields that must keep personal data into a separately access-controlled store, and stop outputs holding sensitive personal data from being kept past the task. Attach the redaction rules per pipeline and a redacted sample from each.

evidenceHint.en: Redaction rules for each logging pipeline and transcript store, a sample of redacted entries, and the retention setting for outputs holding sensitive personal data

text.en: List every pipeline and store that persists prompts, responses or tool output.
Add a scrubbing step before each write that replaces listed identifiers with tokens.
Route fields that must keep personal data to a separate store with restricted access.
Set stored outputs flagged as holding sensitive personal data to expire when the task ends.
Export a redacted sample from each pipeline as proof the rules apply.

title.en: Monitor personal data blocks raised by the response filter and DLP service

description.en: Go through the period's events where a response was masked or blocked for personal data: confirm whether each caught a real identifier, trace repeat events to the document, tool result or input that put the identifier in front of the agent, and send false positives and source fixes to the rule owner. Attach the block register with each event's disposition.

evidenceHint.en: Register of personal data block and mask events for the period, giving identifier type, its source and the disposition of each

text.en: Export the period's block and mask events from the filter and the DLP console.
Confirm whether each event caught a real personal identifier.
Trace repeat events to the document, tool or input that carried the identifier.
Send false positives and source fixes to the rule owner, naming who will act.
Close each event with its disposition and the reviewer's name.

title.en: Sample log stores and transcripts for personal identifiers that escaped redaction

description.en: Draw a random sample of log lines and stored transcripts from each pipeline in the period and scan it for every identifier on the list; then pass synthetic personal records through the agent and confirm each prompt, response and log entry is handled as the list sets. Attach the sample, the scan results and every escaped identifier with its fix.

evidenceHint.en: Log and transcript sample with scan results, synthetic-record results per identifier, and each escaped identifier with its fix and owner

text.en: Pull a random sample of log lines and transcripts from every pipeline.
Scan the sample with the detector and with a second, independent pattern set.
Run synthetic records covering every listed identifier through the agent end to end.
Compare the observed handling on each path with the identifier list.
Enter each escaped identifier with the pipeline at fault, its fix and its owner.

templates.title: Agent outputs kept from infringing third parties' copyrights and trademarks
templates.description: For an externally facing agent, the organisation knows what infringement indemnity each model provider gives and on what conditions, adds copyright and trademark screening where that protection leaves gaps, warns users before operations that carry infringement risk, and writes IP restrictions into its usage policy. The subject is rights belonging to others, not the organisation's own IP.
templates.defaultOwnerHint: Legal Counsel / Product Engineering Lead
templates.objective: To keep what an externally facing agent produces from infringing copyright, trademarks or other intellectual property rights that belong to third parties.
templates.successCriteria:
The output types and use cases in which third-party copyright or trademark infringement could arise are identified.
Each model provider's indemnity is on file with its scope, conditions, caps and exclusions, and the use cases it leaves uncovered are named.
Where a gap is named, outputs are screened for protected text, code, images or marks, and each match is resolved.
Users see a warning before high-risk operations, and the usage policy states the IP restrictions.
The deployed configuration meets every condition the provider indemnities attach.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the register of output types and use cases carrying third-party infringement risk.
Obtain each model provider's contract, terms or AI addendum sections on IP indemnity, with conditions, caps and exclusions.
Obtain the screening configuration and the register of screen matches resolved in the period.
Obtain screenshots of the in-product warnings and the usage policy's IP clauses.
Obtain the record of the indemnity-conditions check.

Analysis:
Read each indemnity, list what it excludes, and compare the exclusions with the risk register to confirm each gap is screened, restricted or accepted by a named owner.
Inspect the deployed configuration — provider content filters, model versions, features in use — against each indemnity condition.
Submit a sample of requests for well-known protected works and marks, and confirm the screen or the provider guardrail catches each one.
Sample the screen-match register and confirm each match has a resolution.
Confirm the warnings appear at the operations the risk register marks high risk.

Output:
A per-provider statement of indemnity scope and of conditions met and unmet.
A gap table showing each uncovered use case and whether it is screened, restricted or accepted.
The screening test results and the matches left unresolved.

title.en: Identify the agent outputs and use cases that risk infringing third-party copyright or marks

description.en: With product engineering, list what the externally facing agent produces — prose, code, images, audio, translations — and the use cases in which infringing someone else's rights is plausible: reproducing long passages, lyrics or code under restrictive licences, generating logos, brand names or characters, or imitating a named work. Note for each the protected material it could reproduce. Attach the register.

evidenceHint.en: Register of output types and use cases with plausible third-party copyright or trademark exposure, noting the protected material each could reproduce

text.en: List each kind of output the agent returns to external users.
Name the use cases that could reproduce protected text, code, images or audio.
Name the use cases that could generate other parties' brand names, logos or characters.
Mark the domains where generation should be restricted outright.
Date the register and name who compiled it with product engineering.

title.en: Obtain each model provider's infringement indemnity with its conditions and exclusions

description.en: From each foundation model provider's contract, terms or AI addendum, extract what the provider promises if its output infringes a third party's rights: copyright and trademark coverage, any guardrails it applies, liability caps, the conditions the customer must meet to stay covered, and what is excluded. Compare the coverage with the use-case register and name each gap. Attach the indemnity register and the gap list.

evidenceHint.en: Register of provider IP indemnities giving coverage, conditions, caps and exclusions with contract references, and the list of use cases left uncovered

text.en: Collect the current contract, terms and AI addendum for each model provider.
Extract the indemnity's coverage for copyright claims and for trademark claims.
List the conditions for staying covered, such as keeping provider filters switched on.
List the exclusions and caps, including any for modified models or user-supplied input.
