The owner confirms or removes each person against the role matrix and writes a reason for every change, with AI-specific context such as why someone needs model access, why their right to change an agent's capability boundaries was granted or withdrawn, or why they may read sensitive prompt and response history. Raise a ticket for each removal or change and see it completed. Attach the review record and its tickets.

evidenceHint.en: Quarterly access review record listing each person, resource and decision with its reason, and the tickets that carried out each removal or change

text.en: Export every person holding access to each inventoried AI system resource.
Have each resource owner confirm or remove each person against the role matrix.
Write a reason for each change, such as the need for model or prompt-log access.
Update the matrix where a policy or role change has made an entry wrong.
Raise a ticket for every removal or change the review decides and close it when done.

title.en: Compare live AI system permissions with the role matrix and the review's decided removals

description.en: After each quarterly review closes, export current permissions and compare them with the role matrix and the review's decisions, and check the quarter's leavers and movers against the export. As a test, try to open a sensitive resource such as the prompt logs from an account whose role should not reach it. Attach the comparison and the test result, with each mismatch, its fix and owner.

evidenceHint.en: Post-review comparison of live permissions against the role matrix and the review's decisions, with leaver and mover checks, the refused-access test and each mismatch's fix

text.en: Export current permissions for every inventoried resource once the review closes.
Confirm each removal the review decided is absent from the export.
Check the quarter's leavers and movers for access their new status does not allow.
Try to open the prompt logs from an account whose role excludes them.
Log each mismatch with its fix, owner and target date.

templates.title: Every caller of the AI system's APIs and agent interfaces authenticated over an encrypted channel
templates.description: The environment serving the AI system authenticates every caller of its model APIs, MCP servers and agent-to-agent interfaces, using scoped tokens, validated OIDC tokens, signed requests or mutual authentication, and carries that traffic over TLS. Where proportionate it also verifies model artefacts before loading them, signs agent-to-agent messages and serves models from minimal, scanned and isolated hosts.
templates.defaultOwnerHint: Platform Security Lead / Infrastructure Engineering
templates.objective: To ensure no caller reaches the AI system's APIs or agent interfaces without proving who it is over an encrypted channel, and that the models served there have not been tampered with.
templates.successCriteria:
Every model API, MCP endpoint and agent-to-agent interface is registered with the authentication and transport it requires.
Each interface rejects a caller without a valid, correctly scoped token, signature or client certificate.
All traffic on those interfaces uses TLS, and plaintext connections are refused or redirected.
Long-lived service credentials on MCP and agent-to-agent connections have a rotation period and were rotated within it.
Where proportionate, model artefacts are hash- or signature-checked and scanned before deployment, on hosts built from minimal, scanned images.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the interface register listing each model API, MCP endpoint and agent-to-agent interface with its authentication and transport settings.
Obtain the authentication middleware, gateway or server configuration for each interface, and its TLS configuration and certificates.
Obtain the credential rotation policy and the rotation log for long-lived service credentials in the period.
Obtain the model deployment pipeline configuration for integrity checks and image scanning, and deployment logs carrying model hashes, where these are in use.

Analysis:
Compare the register with gateway and load-balancer listeners to find exposed interfaces it omits.
Call a sample of interfaces with no credential, an expired token and a token scoped for another resource, and confirm each call is refused.
Attempt a plaintext connection to each sampled interface and confirm it is refused or redirected.
Compare the rotation log with the rotation policy and list credentials older than their period.
Where integrity checks are in use, compare deployed model hashes with the approved values and read the latest image scans for unresolved findings.

Output:
A list of interfaces missing from the register or accepting unauthenticated, wrongly scoped or plaintext connections.
A list of service credentials past their rotation period.
A statement of whether deployed model artefacts match their approved hashes, noting open image vulnerabilities.

title.en: Enumerate the model APIs, MCP endpoints and agent-to-agent interfaces that accept callers

description.en: List every interface through which a person, service or agent can call the AI system: model inference APIs, MCP servers it exposes, agent-to-agent endpoints, webhooks and admin APIs. For each, note who or what calls it, the authentication it requires, the transport it uses and any long-lived credential behind it, and check the list against gateway and load-balancer listeners so nothing exposed is missed. Attach the interface register with its date.

evidenceHint.en: Interface register naming each model API, MCP endpoint, agent-to-agent interface and admin API with its callers, authentication, transport and long-lived credentials

text.en: List the model inference APIs, exposed MCP servers, agent-to-agent endpoints and admin APIs.
Note the callers of each interface: people, internal services or other agents.
Write down the authentication method and transport each interface requires today.
Name any long-lived credential a service connection relies on.
Check the register against gateway and load-balancer listeners for omissions.

title.en: Enforce caller authentication with scoped tokens, signed requests or mutual TLS on each interface

description.en: Put authentication in front of every interface in the register. Model APIs accept only a request carrying a scoped token or a valid request signature; MCP connections have their OAuth 2.0 or OIDC tokens validated, audience and scope included; agent-to-agent interfaces authenticate both ends, for example with mutual TLS. Where the deployment calls for it, sign agent-to-agent messages and verify each signature on receipt. Attach the authentication configuration for each interface.

evidenceHint.en: Authentication configuration per interface: token scoping or request signing for model APIs, OIDC validation for MCP connections, mutual authentication on agent-to-agent links and their signed messages where used

text.en: Issue scoped API tokens or request-signing keys to each model API caller.
Validate issuer, audience, expiry and scope on every OIDC token an MCP connection presents.
Configure mutual authentication on each agent-to-agent interface.
Sign agent-to-agent messages and reject unsigned ones where the deployment calls for it.
Close any anonymous or shared-key access path the register uncovered.

title.en: Configure TLS on every model API, MCP and agent-to-agent channel and refuse plaintext

description.en: Turn on TLS wherever the interface register shows a caller connecting, internal MCP and agent-to-agent links included, because those carry tokens and prompts even when they never leave the network. Set the accepted protocol versions and ciphers at the load balancer or server, make plaintext requests fail or redirect, and track each certificate through to its expiry. Attach the TLS configuration and the certificate inventory.

evidenceHint.en: TLS configuration and certificate inventory for each interface, internal MCP and agent-to-agent links included, showing protocol versions, plaintext refusal and certificate expiry

text.en: Enable TLS on every registered interface, internal MCP and agent-to-agent links included.
Disable outdated protocol versions and weak cipher suites in the TLS settings.
Refuse or redirect plaintext connections on each interface.
List each certificate with its expiry date and the interface it serves.

title.en: Verify model artefact hashes and scan model-serving images before each deployment

description.en: Where proportionate, add checks to the model deployment pipeline: compare each model file's hash or signature with the value stored when it was approved for use, scan serialised model files for embedded code, and build model-serving containers from minimal, current base images scanned for known vulnerabilities. Choose the isolation for each model host by its risk, such as separate namespaces, virtual machines or dedicated GPUs. Attach the pipeline configuration and a deployment log showing the model hash.

evidenceHint.en: Deployment pipeline configuration showing model hash or signature checks, model-file scanning and image vulnerability scanning, plus a deployment log recording model hashes

text.en: Store the hash or signature of each model artefact when it is approved for use.
Fail the deployment when a model file's hash or signature does not match.
Scan serialised model files, such as pickle files, for embedded executable code.
Build model-serving images from minimal base images and scan them for known flaws.
Choose namespace, virtual machine or dedicated GPU isolation for each model host by risk.

title.en: Rotate the long-lived credentials behind MCP and agent-to-agent service connections

description.en: Write a rotation policy giving a period for each type of long-lived service credential on MCP and agent-to-agent connections, then rotate each credential named in the interface register at that period. Issue the replacement, move the connection onto it, revoke the old value once nothing uses it, and log each rotation with the credential, the date and who carried it out. Attach the rotation policy and the rotation log for the period.

evidenceHint.en: Rotation policy for long-lived MCP and agent-to-agent service credentials, and the rotation log giving each credential, its rotation date and the revocation of the old value

text.en: Write the rotation period for each type of long-lived service credential in the policy.
Issue the replacement credential and move the service connection onto it.
Revoke the old credential once the connection runs on the new one.
Log each rotation with the credential, the date and the person who carried it out.

title.en: Exercise each exposed interface with unauthenticated, wrongly scoped and plaintext connection attempts

description.en: Once a year, take every interface in the register and try to call it with no credential, with an expired token, with a token scoped for another resource and over plaintext, confirming each attempt is refused. Compare the register with current gateway listeners for newly exposed interfaces, and the rotation log with the policy for overdue credentials. Attach the test results with each failure, its fix and owner.

evidenceHint.en: Interface test results for unauthenticated, expired-token, wrongly scoped and plaintext attempts, with unregistered interfaces, overdue credentials and each failure's fix

text.en: Call each registered interface with no credential and confirm it is refused.
Repeat the call with an expired token and with one scoped for another resource.
Attempt a plaintext connection to each interface and confirm it fails.
Compare gateway listeners with the register for interfaces it does not list.
List credentials past their rotation period from the rotation log.

templates.title: Agent output capped in volume and precision so it cannot be mined for reconstruction
templates.description: For agents that generate text, speech or images, each output path caps tokens or characters, results returned and inference time, and responses whose precision would let repeated queries rebuild underlying data or the model — exact figures, raw confidence scores — are rounded, banded or withheld where the use case calls for it. Users are told when an answer was truncated or coarsened.
templates.defaultOwnerHint: AI Platform Lead / Security Engineering
templates.objective: To limit how much, and how precisely, the agent discloses in each response, so outputs cannot be harvested to rebuild sensitive data or the model behind them.
templates.successCriteria:
Every output path is listed with the data or model behaviour its volume or precision could expose and the limit legitimate users need.
Each path enforces a token or character cap, a result-count cap and an inference time limit, and over-limit requests stop at the cap or time out.
Where the use case calls for it, sensitive figures and confidence scores are rounded, banded or withheld before they reach the user.
A user whose answer was truncated, suppressed or coarsened sees a notice saying so, and help documentation explains the limits.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the list of output paths with the exposure and the limits assigned to each.
Obtain the configuration setting token or character caps, result-count caps and inference timeouts on each path.
Obtain the code applying rounding, banding or suppression to sensitive figures and scores.
Obtain screenshots of truncation and coarsening notices and the help article describing output limits.

Analysis:
Compare the listed paths with the endpoints, tools and response templates in the deployed system to find paths without limits.
For each path, send requests designed to exceed every cap and confirm the response stops at the configured limit or times out.
Request sensitive figures and scores at full precision and compare the returned values with the rounding or banding defined.
Trigger each kind of limit and confirm the user notice appears.
Repeat a sample of high-precision requests and judge whether combining the answers recovers precision the banding removes.

Output:
A path-by-path table of configured against observed limits.
A list of paths without caps, of figures returned at full precision, and of limits applied without a user notice.
A judgement on whether repeated responses recover withheld precision.

title.en: Identify each output path whose volume or precision could expose data or the model

description.en: List the ways the agent hands information back — chat responses, retrieval result lists, generated documents, speech, images, exports, numeric scores — and note for each what could be rebuilt from long or exact output: records in the underlying data, sensitive figures, or the model's decision behaviour. Note beside it the length, result count and precision legitimate users need, so the caps balance security with usefulness. Attach the list with its date.

evidenceHint.en: List of output paths giving the data or model behaviour each could expose and the output volume and precision legitimate users need

text.en: List each response channel, tool result and export the agent returns to users.
Note the data or model behaviour each could reveal if its output were long or exact.
Set out the length, result count and precision legitimate users need on each path.
Mark the paths returning numeric figures or confidence scores for precision limits.
Date the list and link it to the architecture diagram of the response paths.

title.en: Set token, character, result-count and inference-time caps on every output path

description.en: Configure each path from the list with the limits it was given: a maximum number of tokens or characters per response, a maximum number of results or records returned, a time limit on inference after which the request stops, and a limit on speech duration or images per request where the agent produces them. Hold the caps in versioned configuration. Attach the configuration for each path.

evidenceHint.en: Configuration for each output path showing the token or character cap, result-count cap and inference timeout, with the version in force

text.en: Set a maximum token or character count on each response path.
Cap the number of results or records a single response may return.
Configure an inference timeout that ends a request at the agreed limit.
Limit speech duration or images per request where the agent produces them.
Commit the limits to versioned configuration and note the version deployed.

title.en: Limit the precision of sensitive figures and confidence scores returned to users

description.en: Where the use case calls for it, coarsen output whose precision would make it exploitable: round figures derived from sensitive data, report scores or probabilities in bands rather than exact values, and withhold raw confidence scores and token probabilities, so repeated querying cannot invert the model or recover underlying values. Set the rounding or band for each figure the output-path list marks. Attach the code and the bands applied.

evidenceHint.en: Code or configuration applying rounding, banding or suppression to each sensitive figure and score, with the precision set for each

text.en: Pick each figure and score the output-path list marks for precision limits.
Set a rounding rule or band edges for each one.
Strip raw confidence scores and token probabilities from user-facing responses.
Apply the coarsening in the response layer after generation and before display.
Store the code with the band table and its version.

title.en: Notify users in the response when output was truncated, suppressed or coarsened

description.en: Where the deployment calls for it, add a short notice to any response that hit a cap, timed out, had results suppressed or had figures banded, saying in general terms what was limited and why, and publish a help article describing the limits users can expect. Attach screenshots of each notice and the help article.

evidenceHint.en: Screenshots of the notice shown for each kind of limit — truncation, timeout, suppression, banding — and the published help article on output limits

text.en: Write a notice for each limit type: truncated, timed out, suppressed and banded.
Append the matching notice to the response whenever a limit fires.
Publish a help article explaining the output limits users may meet.
Capture a screenshot of each notice in the live product.

title.en: Test each output path with over-limit and high-precision requests

description.en: Send each path requests built to exceed every cap — very long answers, large result sets, slow generations — and requests for sensitive figures at full precision, then repeat a sample to see whether combining answers recovers precision the banding removed. Compare what came back with the configured limits and confirm the notice appeared. Attach the test log with every gap.

evidenceHint.en: Test log per output path with configured and observed limits, the precision results, the repeated-query result and each gap with its owner

text.en: Write over-limit requests for each cap on each path.
Run them and note where output stopped, timed out or was truncated.
Request sensitive figures at full precision and compare them with the bands.
Repeat a sample of requests and check whether combining answers recovers precision.
Enter each gap with the path, the limit at fault and the owner of the fix.

templates.title: Agent-generated code defaults to safe queries, vetted auth libraries and pinned, real dependencies
templates.description: Instructions, scaffolding and checks around the agent's code generation make the secure pattern the one it reaches for unprompted: injection-safe data access, escaped rendering and encrypted transport; vetted libraries for sign-in and access checks; dependencies that exist, are maintained and are pinned. Where proportionate the same holds for sessions, input validation, error handling and logging. Applies to agents that generate code.
templates.defaultOwnerHint: Application Security Lead / AI Platform Engineering Lead
templates.objective: To make the code the agent writes secure by default, so a user who never asks for safe patterns still receives injection-safe, properly authorised code with trustworthy dependencies.
templates.successCriteria:
The code-generation instructions or scaffolding direct the model to parameterised data access, contextual escaping and TLS for every language and framework in scope.
Generated sign-in and authorisation code uses established libraries and deny-by-default checks, and the agent writes no cryptographic or authentication primitives of its own.
Every package the agent adds to a manifest carries a pinned version, exists in its registry and is absent from the deny list.
A sample of generations on data, auth, dependency and logging prompts shows the secure pattern used unasked.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the inventory of code-generation surfaces with the languages, frameworks and package ecosystems each one covers.
Obtain the system prompt sections, scaffolding templates and post-generation checks that set secure defaults, with their version history for the period.
Obtain the registry-check configuration, its refusal log and the dated versions of the package deny list.
Obtain the organisation's own sample generations and their static-analysis results for the period.

Analysis:
Map each inventoried language and framework to the defaults covering injection, rendering, transport, authentication and dependencies, and note any left uncovered.
Draw a fresh sample of prompts per surface across data access, UI rendering, sign-in, access control, manifests and logging, run them with no security wording, and inspect the code returned.
Run a static analyser over the sampled code and compare its findings with the organisation's own results.
Check each sampled manifest for wildcard or floating versions and for package names absent from their registry.

Output:
A coverage table of surface and language against each secure default, naming the gaps.
The sample results, listing each insecure pattern found with its prompt and surface.
A list of manifest entries that were unpinned, nonexistent or on the deny list.

title.en: Inventory the code-generation surfaces, languages and package ecosystems the agent writes for

description.en: Secure defaults are set per language and framework, so start by listing where the agent produces code — chat code blocks, an editor assistant, project scaffolding, commits or pull requests it opens — and, for each surface, the languages, frameworks and package ecosystems it commonly emits. Note which surfaces run on a third-party model or coding platform and which of their instructions you control. Attach the dated inventory.

evidenceHint.en: Inventory of code-generation surfaces, one row per surface, naming its languages, frameworks, package ecosystems and who controls its instructions

text.en: List each product surface where the agent writes code a user may keep or run.
Note the languages and frameworks each surface emits, taken from usage data or product scope.
Name the package ecosystems each surface can add dependencies from, such as npm or PyPI.
Mark surfaces that run on a provider's model or platform and the settings you control there.
Sign and date the inventory so the annual sample can be drawn against it.

title.en: Set secure defaults for database access, rendered markup and network calls in generated code

description.en: Write the defaults into the system prompt or coding instructions for every inventoried language, and into any scaffolding templates the agent fills: database access through parameterised queries or the framework's query builder, user data rendered through auto-escaping templates or contextual encoding, and outbound calls over HTTPS with certificate checks left on. Where proportionate, add validation of user-supplied input, error responses that hide stack traces, rate limits on public endpoints and log statements that leave out auth headers and full request bodies. Attach the instruction excerpts and templates.

evidenceHint.en: Coding-instruction excerpts and scaffolding templates showing the default for data access, rendering and transport and, where adopted, for validation, errors and logging

text.en: Add parameterised-query or query-builder guidance for each inventoried language to the instructions.
Set scaffolding templates to auto-escape rendered user data, encoding by context where they cannot.
Instruct the model to use HTTPS with certificate verification on for every outbound call it writes.
Add input validation, generic error responses and endpoint rate limits where the deployment calls for it.
Direct generated logging to omit auth headers, request bodies and sensitive fields, where proportionate.
Version the instructions and templates so each change appears in their history.

title.en: Restrict generated authentication and authorisation code to vetted libraries and deny-by-default checks

description.en: Name, for each inventoried framework, the established authentication library or framework-native mechanism the agent should use, and instruct the model to place an authorisation check on every route or handler it writes, granting least privilege and denying when no rule matches. Forbid hand-rolled password hashing, token signing, encryption and session handling. Where the deployment calls for it, default session cookies to HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite and add CSRF protection to state-changing endpoints. Attach the instruction excerpts and the library list.

evidenceHint.en: Approved authentication library list per framework, and instruction excerpts covering access checks, banned home-made primitives and, where adopted, cookie and CSRF defaults

text.en: Choose the approved authentication library or native mechanism for each inventoried framework.
Instruct the model to add an access check to every generated route and deny when no rule matches.
Forbid home-made password hashing, token signing and encryption in the coding instructions.
Default generated session cookies to HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite where the deployment calls for it.
Add CSRF protection to generated state-changing endpoints where proportionate.

title.en: Enforce pinned versions and registry-verified package names in manifests the agent generates

description.en: Instruct the model to give every dependency an exact or bounded version and never a wildcard or 'latest'. Add a check that runs on each generated manifest or install command, looks every package up in its registry, and refuses or flags a name that does not exist, has been abandoned or appears on the deny list of lookalike names. Log each refusal with the package and ecosystem. Attach the instruction excerpt, the check's configuration and an example refusal from its log.

evidenceHint.en: Dependency instruction excerpt, registry-check configuration covering each ecosystem, and a logged example of a refused package

text.en: Add a rule to the coding instructions requiring a pinned version for every dependency.
Build a check that looks up each generated package name in its registry before output.
Refuse or flag names missing from the registry, abandoned upstream or on the deny list.
Log each refusal with the package name, its ecosystem and the surface that produced it.
Cover every package ecosystem named in the code-generation inventory.

title.en: Refresh the abandoned and lookalike package deny list from the registry check's refusals

description.en: On the cadence the team sets, read the registry check's refusal log and each ecosystem's advisories on removed, hijacked or abandoned packages, and add the abandoned and lookalike names to the deny list that the check and the coding instructions both use. Remove entries that no longer apply, giving the reason. Attach each dated version of the deny list with what changed and the refusal-log extract it drew on.

evidenceHint.en: Dated versions of the package deny list with additions and removals, and the refusal-log extract each change drew on

text.en: Export the refusal log entries since the previous deny-list update.
Check each ecosystem's advisories for packages removed, taken over or marked abandoned.
Add new abandoned and lookalike names to the deny list with their source.
Remove entries that no longer apply and note why each was removed.
Release the updated list to the registry check and the coding instructions together.

title.en: Sample generations on database, sign-in, dependency and logging prompts for insecure patterns

description.en: Once a year, write a set of ordinary prompts for each inventoried surface — a query, a form that renders user data, a login flow, an admin route, a new manifest, a logging helper — with no mention of security, run them, and pass the code returned through a static analyser and a security reviewer. List each insecure pattern found with its prompt and the change to the instructions or templates that fixes it. Attach the prompt set, the generated code and the findings.

evidenceHint.en: Annual sample of prompts and generated code per surface, with static-analysis output, each insecure pattern found and the fix agreed

text.en: Write prompts per surface covering queries, rendering, sign-in, access control, manifests and logging.
Run each prompt without security wording and save the code returned with the model version.
Pass the generated code through a static analyser and a security reviewer.
Check each generated manifest for floating versions and for packages missing from the registry.
List each insecure pattern with its prompt and the instruction or template change that fixes it.

templates.title: AI risk taxonomy graded by severity and built from each agent's capabilities and context
templates.description: A written taxonomy of the ways the organisation's AI agents can cause harm, derived from what each agent can do, who uses it and the industry it serves. Every risk carries a grade on one shared severity scale, a worked example from the deployment and a cross-reference to external frameworks, and the scale sets when output is flagged or sent to a person. It is reviewed at least once a year and changed when incidents or new threats warrant.
templates.defaultOwnerHint: Head of AI Risk / AI Governance Committee
templates.objective: To give every AI testing, guardrail, monitoring and failure-plan activity one current, severity-graded list of the risks each deployed agent actually presents.
templates.successCriteria:
Every risk in the taxonomy has a definition and an example drawn from a deployed agent's own capabilities, users or industry.
One severity scale is applied to all risks, and it states the level that triggers flagging and the level that triggers human review.
Each risk is cross-referenced to the external frameworks the organisation reports against, or marked as having no counterpart.
A review in the last twelve months is on record with its participants, decisions, rationale and approval.
Every change made between reviews has a change-log entry naming the incident, threat or new capability behind it.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the current taxonomy with its version history and approval record.
Obtain the inventory of deployed agents with their capabilities, user populations and deployment context.
Obtain the record of the most recent annual review and the change log since the review before it.
Obtain the incident register and threat-intelligence notes for the period.

Analysis:
Check that every risk has a definition, a grade on the severity scale and an example tied to a named agent.
Compare the severity definitions across categories for a single scale with stated flagging and human-review levels.
Trace each capability in the inventory — taking actions, generating code, reaching personal data, facing the public — to at least one risk, and list capabilities with none.
Sample incidents from the register across the period and confirm each falls under an existing risk or prompted a logged change.
Check the framework cross-references for risks left unmapped without a stated reason.
Confirm the review took place within twelve months of the one before it and that its decisions appear in the version history.

Output:
A risk-by-risk table of definition, grade, example and framework reference, with gaps marked.
A list of agent capabilities and sampled incidents the taxonomy does not cover.
A statement of whether the annual review and the change log are complete for the period.

title.en: Inventory each agent's capabilities, users and deployment context for the taxonomy

description.en: A taxonomy written in the abstract misses the risks a particular agent presents. For every deployed or planned agent, list what it can do — the tools it calls, the actions it takes, whether it writes code, reaches personal data or faces the public — who uses it, including any vulnerable groups, and the industry and jurisdictions it serves. Attach the inventory, one row per agent, with its date and the name of whoever compiled it.

evidenceHint.en: Agent capability and context inventory, one row per agent, listing tools and actions, user populations, industry and jurisdictions

text.en: List each deployed or planned agent and the tools and actions it is permitted to use.
Note whether each agent generates code, reaches personal data or is externally facing.
Describe the user populations served, flagging minors or other vulnerable groups.
Add the industry, jurisdictions and business process each agent operates within.
Date the inventory and pass it to the taxonomy owner for drafting.

title.en: Define risk categories with worked examples from each agent's own deployment

description.en: Write the groups of harm the agents can cause — data and privacy, security, safety, reliability, accountability and wider society — and break each into specific risks the inventory shows are real. Give every specific risk a one-sentence definition and a concrete example from a named agent, such as an agent with refund authority being talked into an unearned refund, and include high-stakes uses like safety-critical instructions or legal and financial recommendations wherever a deployment touches them. Attach the category list.

evidenceHint.en: Taxonomy category list giving every specific risk a definition and an example tied to a named agent's deployment

text.en: Group risks under data and privacy, security, safety, reliability, accountability and society.
Break each group into specific risks the inventory shows an agent could present.
Write a one-sentence definition for every specific risk.
Add an example per risk taken from a named agent's tools, users or industry.
List risks considered and excluded, with the reason each does not apply.

title.en: Set one severity scale for every risk, naming the levels that trigger flagging and review

description.en: Define a single severity scale, each level described by the harm it represents to a user, a customer or the organisation, and grade every taxonomy risk on it, so that a top-grade privacy failure and a top-grade safety failure mean the same thing. State the level at which an occurrence is flagged for investigation and the level at which output must go to a person, set to the organisation's own risk tolerance. Attach the scale, the grade of each risk and the approval of both levels.

evidenceHint.en: Severity scale definitions, the grade assigned to each taxonomy risk, and the approved flagging and human-review levels

text.en: Describe the harm each severity level represents, from the lowest to the highest.
Grade every risk in the category list on that one scale, with a sentence of rationale.
State the severity level at which an occurrence is flagged for investigation.
State the level at which output must be routed to a person before it reaches a user.
Obtain approval of the scale and both levels from the accountable risk owner.

title.en: Cross-reference each taxonomy risk to the external frameworks the organisation reports against

description.en: Map every specific risk to the clauses of the regulations and standards in the organisation's compliance register that address it — risk-management obligations, AI management-system controls, sector rules — so an auditor or regulator can see the taxonomy covers what they expect. Where a framework names a risk the taxonomy lacks, add it or write down why it does not apply. Attach the cross-reference table.

evidenceHint.en: Cross-reference table from each taxonomy risk to external framework clauses, with gaps and how each was disposed of

text.en: Take the AI regulations and standards listed in the organisation's compliance register.
Map each taxonomy risk to the clauses in those frameworks that address it.
List framework risks that have no matching taxonomy entry.
Add each missing risk to the category list or write why it does not apply.
Date the table and file it with the taxonomy version it describes.

title.en: Log taxonomy changes prompted by incidents, emerging threats or new agent capabilities

description.en: Between annual reviews, open a change entry whenever an incident, a near miss, a newly published attack technique or a new agent capability exposes a risk the taxonomy does not hold or grades wrongly. Each entry names the trigger, the change proposed — a risk added, removed, regraded or given a new example — who approved it and the version it took effect in. Attach the change log for the period.

evidenceHint.en: Taxonomy change log listing trigger, change made, approver and resulting version for every change in the period

text.en: Open a change entry when an incident or near miss reveals a missing or misgraded risk.
Open one when a published attack technique could reach the deployed agents.
Open one when an agent gains a tool, action or user population not in the inventory.
Name the change, its approver and the taxonomy version it takes effect in.
Notify the owners of testing, guardrails and monitoring when a new version is issued.

title.en: Review the whole taxonomy annually against the inventory, incident register and change log

description.en: Once a year, bring the risk owner together with engineering, security and legal to read the taxonomy end to end: refresh the capability inventory, check that every incident of the year falls under a risk, confirm the grades still match experience, and decide for each risk whether to keep, change or retire it. Minute the participants, decisions and rationale, approve the resulting version, and attach the minutes with the version history.

evidenceHint.en: Annual review minutes with date, participants, decision and rationale per risk, plus the approved version and its history

text.en: Refresh the agent capability inventory before the review meeting.
Check every incident and near miss from the year against the category list.
Decide for each risk whether to keep, change or retire it, with a rationale.
Minute the participants, the decisions and any change to the flagging or review levels.
Approve and issue the resulting version, and set the date of the next review.

templates.title: Approval-requiring AI changes tested across the taxonomy and signed off before release
templates.description: Before a change that the change-approval rules say needs formal sign-off reaches users — a new model or prompt, a new tool or data source, an altered guardrail — the team that owns it tests it against the risk taxonomy, rates every issue found, fixes or formally accepts each one and obtains release approval. Where proportionate, the tests gate the pipeline, AI artefacts and libraries are scanned, and open-weight model changes are regression-tested.
templates.defaultOwnerHint: AI Engineering Lead / Release Manager
templates.objective: To stop an approval-requiring AI change reaching users until its own team has tested it across the risk taxonomy and an accountable person has accepted the results.
templates.successCriteria:
A written test plan maps each change type that needs approval to the pre-release tests it must pass for each taxonomy category it can affect.
Every approval-requiring change released in the period has test results on file, with each issue found given a severity rating.
Each rated issue has a fix, a mitigation or a recorded acceptance of its residual risk, decided before the release date.
A sign-off from the accountable person, with rationale, predates deployment for every such change.
Where adopted, pipeline gate runs, artefact and library scans and open-weight regression results exist for each release.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the pre-release test plan and the change-approval rules that say which changes need formal sign-off.
Obtain the list of AI system changes deployed in the period from the release history.
Obtain, for each change, the test results, issue list with severities, risk assessment and sign-off.
Where adopted, obtain the pipeline gate configuration and run history, scan outputs and open-weight regression reports.

Analysis:
Filter the release history to the changes the approval rules cover and compare it with the changes holding test records, listing any deployed without one.
Sample covered changes across every change type and confirm the tests run match those the plan requires for that type.
For each sampled change, check every issue has a severity and a fix, mitigation or acceptance, and that the decision and sign-off predate the deployment timestamp.
Read the rationale for each accepted high-severity issue and confirm the approver is the person the approval rules name.
Where a pipeline gate exists, confirm from its run history that failed AI tests blocked promotion or were overridden by a named person with a reason.
For open-weight model changes, compare before-and-after results and confirm each regression was decided on.

Output:
A list of approval-requiring changes deployed without tests, decisions or sign-off.
A per-sample table of tests required against tests run, issues, decisions and sign-off dates.
A note of gate overrides and of open-weight regressions left undecided.

title.en: Write the pre-release test plan linking change types to taxonomy-category test suites

description.en: Take the change types the approval rules say need formal sign-off — a model swap, a system-prompt rewrite, a new tool or data source, a guardrail change — and set out which tests each must pass for every taxonomy category it can affect: hallucination question sets, adversarial and injection prompts, safety unit tests, and scenario walkthroughs of whole agent tasks. Say how results are rated on the taxonomy's severity scale. Attach the plan with its version date.

evidenceHint.en: Pre-release test plan mapping each approval-requiring change type to the test suites and taxonomy categories it must cover

text.en: List the change types the change-approval rules say need formal sign-off.
Name the taxonomy categories each change type can plausibly affect.
Assign hallucination, adversarial, safety unit and scenario tests to each category.
Describe how each issue found is rated on the taxonomy's severity scale.
Store the plan in the repository the delivery team reads before release.

title.en: Configure the release pipeline to block on failed AI tests and vulnerable model artefacts

description.en: Where proportionate to how often the system changes, make the pre-release suite a required check in the CI/CD or MLOps pipeline so an approval-requiring change cannot be promoted while it fails, and add scans of model files and machine-learning libraries for known vulnerabilities and unsafe serialisation. Protect the gate with branch rules so an override needs a named person and leaves a trace. Attach the pipeline configuration and branch protection settings.

evidenceHint.en: Pipeline configuration showing the AI test suite and artefact and library scans as required checks, plus branch protection settings

text.en: Add the pre-release AI test suite as a required job in the deployment pipeline.
Add dependency scanning for the machine-learning libraries the agent imports.
Add a scan of model files for unsafe serialisation and known-vulnerable formats.
Set branch protection so a release cannot merge while a required job fails.
Limit gate overrides to named people and log each override with its reason.

title.en: Run the planned taxonomy tests on each approval-requiring change and rate every issue found

description.en: For each change that needs formal approval, run the tests the plan assigns in a staging environment that mirrors the production tool set and data permissions, and log every issue with the taxonomy category it falls under, its severity and the prompt or trace that reproduces it. Attach the test run output and the issue list for the change.

evidenceHint.en: Test run output for the change, with an issue list giving taxonomy category, severity and reproduction for each issue

text.en: Identify the change type and pull the tests the plan assigns to it.
Run the tests in staging with the production tool set and data permissions.
Walk through the end-to-end scenarios and note behaviour that departs from expectation.
Log each issue with its category, severity and the prompt or trace reproducing it.
Link the test output and issue list to the change ticket.

title.en: Obtain release sign-off on each change's rated issues, mitigations and accepted residual risk

description.en: Before deployment, assess each rated issue for its possible impact on users and the business, decide whether it is fixed, mitigated or accepted, and state the residual risk that remains. Put the issue list, decisions and residual risk before the accountable person the approval rules name for that change type, and obtain a sign-off that gives the reason for releasing. Attach the risk assessment and the dated sign-off.

evidenceHint.en: Risk assessment of each issue with its fix, mitigation or acceptance and residual risk, and the accountable person's dated sign-off with rationale

text.en: Write the possible impact of each issue on users, customers and the organisation.
Decide for each issue whether it is fixed, mitigated or accepted before release.
State the residual risk of every issue that is mitigated or accepted rather than fixed.
Present the decisions to the approver the change-approval rules name for this type.
File the dated sign-off and its rationale on the change ticket before deploying.

title.en: Compare a changed open-weight model's safety and guardrail results with its prior baseline

description.en: Where the deployment runs an open-weight model, treat new weights from fine-tuning or quantisation, or a change of inference engine, as a model change: re-run the safety evaluations and guardrail suites on the new version, compare each taxonomy category's results with the previous version's baseline, and apply lighter automated checks to changes the plan classes as routine or low-risk. Attach the before-and-after results naming both model versions.

evidenceHint.en: Regression report naming the prior and new model versions, the taxonomy categories tested and before-and-after results

text.en: Name the prior and new model versions and what changed: weights, quantisation or engine.
Re-run the safety evaluation and guardrail suites on the new version.
Compare each taxonomy category's results with the prior version's baseline.
Raise each regression as a rated issue for the release decision.
Run only the plan's automated checks for changes it classes as routine or low-risk.

title.en: Reconcile deployed AI changes against pre-release test records and sign-off dates

description.en: At the end of the period, export every AI system change deployed from the release history, filter it to those the approval rules cover, and check each has test results, rated issues, decisions and a sign-off dated before deployment. Investigate every change that shipped without them and every gate override, and agree a fix. Attach the reconciliation with each exception and its owner.

evidenceHint.en: Reconciliation of deployed approval-requiring changes against test results, decisions and sign-off dates, with exceptions and owners

text.en: Export every AI system change deployed in the period from the release history.
Filter to the changes the change-approval rules required to be approved.
Match each to its test output, issue list, risk assessment and sign-off.
Compare each sign-off date with the deployment timestamp.
List gate overrides and changes shipped without records, with an owner for each fix.

templates.title: Hostile, distressing, offensive, biased or deceptive replies and dangerous advice stopped before delivery
templates.description: An output filter screens each reply for distressing, hostile or offensive language, biased treatment of people and deceptive claims, and blocks or rewrites what it catches; guardrails limit the advice the agent gives in sensitive domains and add warnings where it may advise. Where proportionate, the organisation tests for bias and measures how often the filter blocks wrongly or misses harm. Applies to agents that generate text, speech or images.
templates.defaultOwnerHint: Trust & Safety Lead / AI Platform Engineering Lead
templates.objective: To stop agent replies that could hurt, demean, mislead or endanger a user from being delivered, and to know from measurement how well the controls that stop them work.
templates.successCriteria:
Each harm category the filter covers has a written definition, example replies, a configured threshold and a block or rewrite action.
Every reply passes through the output filter before delivery, and one that crosses a threshold is blocked or rewritten as configured.
Advice in each sensitive domain the agent touches stays within what its guardrail permits and carries the warning set for that domain.
False-positive and miss rates are measured per harm category on a labelled set, and a fix is recorded for each weakness found.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the harm category definitions with their example replies, thresholds and actions.
Obtain the output filter configuration, and the guardrail instructions and warning templates for each sensitive domain, with change history for the period.
Obtain the labelled evaluation set, the filter performance results and any bias evaluation results for the period.
Obtain the filter log of blocked and rewritten replies for the period.

Analysis:
Confirm from the architecture and configuration that every reply path, streamed replies included, passes through the filter.
Send a set of crafted prompts per harm category and per sensitive domain, and compare each reply with the configured action and warning.
Recompute the false-positive and miss rates from the labelled results and compare them with the figures reported.
Sample blocked and rewritten replies from the filter log and judge whether each was in fact harmful.
Where a bias evaluation was run, check that its prompts differed only in the demographic attribute under test.

Output:
A table of harm categories and sensitive domains giving configured action against observed behaviour.
The recomputed performance rates per category beside the reported ones.
A list of reply paths that bypass the filter, harmful replies delivered and safe replies wrongly blocked.

title.en: Define the harm categories the output filter screens for, with replies either side of the line

description.en: Write an operational definition for each kind of harmful reply the filter must catch — distressing content, hostile or angry language, offensive material, biased statements about people, deceptive or manipulative claims, and dangerous advice — with example replies that cross the line and ones that fall just short, so engineers can set thresholds and labellers can judge results consistently. Draw on the risk taxonomy where it already names a category. Attach the definitions with their examples.

evidenceHint.en: Harm category definitions for the output filter, each with replies that cross the line, replies that fall short, and the intended action

text.en: Write a definition for each harm category the output filter must catch.
Add replies that cross the line and replies that fall just short for each category.
Cross-reference each category to the risk taxonomy entry it draws on, where one exists.
State for each category whether a reply is withheld outright or may be rewritten.
Circulate the definitions to the engineers and labellers who will apply them.

title.en: Configure the output moderation classifier's thresholds and block-or-rewrite action per harm category

description.en: Put a moderation classifier, a provider's moderation endpoint or a rule set on the response path so every reply is scored against each defined category before it is delivered, streamed replies included. Set a threshold per category and the action taken at it — withhold the reply and send a safe message, or rewrite it — and log each action with the category and score. Attach the configuration and an example log entry.

evidenceHint.en: Output filter configuration showing the classifier, per-category thresholds and actions, plus a logged example of a blocked or rewritten reply

text.en: Place the classifier or moderation endpoint on every response path, streamed replies included.
Set a threshold for each defined harm category, calibrated on its example replies.
Configure the safe message or rewrite applied when a reply crosses a threshold.
Log each blocked or rewritten reply with its category and score.
Version the configuration so threshold changes appear in its history.

title.en: Set the advice limits and warning text for medical, legal, financial and other sensitive domains

description.en: For each sensitive domain the agent may engage with at all — health, law, money and any other the deployment touches — decide what it may say, what it must refuse to recommend, and the warning it adds when it gives general guidance, such as pointing the user to a qualified professional. Work with engineering to turn those decisions into defensive prompting, domain rules and conditional warning templates. Attach the per-domain limits and the configured prompts and templates.

evidenceHint.en: Per-domain advice limits with refusal rules and warning wording, and the system prompt and template excerpts that apply them

text.en: List the sensitive domains the agent may engage with, including those it should only touch lightly.
State per domain what the agent may say and the recommendations it must refuse.
Write the warning text added when the agent gives general guidance in each domain.
Have engineering apply the limits as defensive prompts, domain rules and warning templates.
Try one crafted request per domain against the configured limits before sign-off.

title.en: Run a paired-prompt bias evaluation that varies only the demographic attribute in each request

description.en: Where proportionate to the deployment, build sets of prompts that are identical except for one demographic attribute — name, gender, age, ethnicity, religion, disability — run them through the agent, and compare the replies for differences in tone, refusals, recommendations and stereotyping. Log each disparity with the fix agreed in the filter, prompts or model choice. Attach the prompt sets, the results by attribute and the fixes.

evidenceHint.en: Bias evaluation prompt sets, results compared by demographic attribute, and the disparities found with their agreed fixes

text.en: Choose the demographic attributes relevant to the people the agent serves.
Write prompt sets that differ only in that attribute and cover the agent's main tasks.
Run each set and save the replies with the model and prompt versions used.
Compare replies across attributes for differences in tone, refusal and recommendation.
Log each disparity found with the fix agreed and its owner.

title.en: Measure the output filter's false-positive and miss rates per harm category on a labelled set

description.en: Where proportionate, assemble a labelled set of harmful and harmless replies for every category — public harm benchmarks where they fit, plus examples drawn from the agent's own traffic — pass it through the filter as configured, and compute the false-positive and miss rate per category. Compare the results with the previous measurement and agree a fix for any category that has worsened or misses harm its definition says it must catch. Attach the dataset description, the rates and the fixes.

evidenceHint.en: Filter performance report giving false-positive and miss rates per harm category, the labelled set used, and the fixes agreed

text.en: Assemble labelled harmful and harmless replies for every defined harm category.
Run the set through the filter exactly as it is configured in production.
Compute false-positive and miss rates per category and save the confusion matrix.
Compare each rate with the previous measurement and flag categories that worsened.
Agree a fix, owner and date for each weak category and add it to the backlog.

templates.title: Agent declines and redirects requests outside the purpose it was deployed for
templates.description: A written scope says what the agent is for and which subjects it declines — a political opinion or medical guidance from an agent built for something else. System prompt rules and topic detection turn those requests away with a redirection message, attempts are logged by topic and frequency and used to adjust the boundaries, and users are told, where proportionate, what the agent does. Applies to agents that generate text or speech.
templates.defaultOwnerHint: Product Owner for the Agent / AI Platform Engineering Lead
templates.objective: To keep the agent answering only the requests it was deployed for and redirecting users who ask for anything else, using logged attempts to adjust where the boundary sits.
templates.successCriteria:
A dated scope statement lists the agent's intended purposes and the subjects it declines, each with an example request.
The agent recognises requests outside its scope and answers them with the redirection message, and repeated attempts in a session trigger the rule set for them.
Every declined request is logged with its topic, and attempt counts per topic are reported for the period.
Each boundary change made in the period cites the attempt pattern that prompted it.
Where user guidance exists, it describes the same purposes and declined subjects as the scope statement.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the scope statement with its intended purposes, declined subjects and example requests.
Obtain the system prompt, topic classifier or blocklist configuration, redirection messages and the repeated-attempt rule.
Obtain the out-of-scope request log and the frequency report for the period.
Obtain the change history for the declined-topic list and redirection rules, and any user-facing guidance on scope.

Analysis:
Send a set of requests for each declined subject, including rephrased, role-play and multi-turn attempts, and check each is declined with the redirection message.
Send in-scope requests close to each boundary and check they are answered rather than wrongly declined.
Repeat an out-of-scope attempt within one session beyond the configured count and confirm the repeated-attempt rule fires.
Reconcile a sample of logged attempts with the frequency report.
Match each boundary change in the period to the attempt pattern it cites.
Compare any user guidance with the scope statement.

Output:
A table of declined subjects with the test requests sent, the responses observed and pass or fail.
A list of in-scope requests wrongly declined.
A list of boundary changes with and without a cited pattern, and of differences between guidance and scope.

title.en: State the purposes the agent is deployed for and the subjects it must decline, with examples

description.en: With the business owner of the deployment, write down what the agent is for — the tasks and audiences it serves — and the subjects it must decline because they fall outside that purpose, such as political opinions or health guidance from an agent built for billing questions. Give an example request for each, including ones close to the line, so engineering and testers share one reading, and say how a user who keeps pushing should be treated. Attach the dated scope statement.

evidenceHint.en: Dated scope statement listing intended purposes, declined subjects, example requests on each side of the boundary and the repeated-attempt rule

text.en: List the tasks and audiences the agent is deployed to serve.
Name the subjects outside that purpose that the agent must decline.
Write example requests for each purpose and declined subject, including near-boundary cases.
Say how the agent treats a user who keeps pushing past the boundary in one session.
Date the statement and file it where engineering and testers will find it.

title.en: Configure topic detection and a redirection reply for requests outside the agent's purpose

description.en: Turn the scope statement into controls: allowed topics and refusals in the system prompt, defensive instructions against role-play or rephrasing used to drag the agent off topic, and a topic classifier or blocklist where prompting alone does not hold. Give each declined subject a redirection message saying what the agent can help with, and apply the statement's rule for users who keep pushing in one session, escalating or restricting further replies. Attach the configuration and message templates.

evidenceHint.en: System prompt excerpt, topic classifier or blocklist configuration, redirection message templates and the repeated-attempt rule

text.en: Write the allowed topics and declined subjects into the system prompt.
Add defensive instructions against role-play and rephrasing used to leave scope.
Configure a topic classifier or blocklist where prompting alone lets requests through.
Write a redirection message per declined subject naming what the agent can help with.
Configure the repeated-attempt rule from the scope statement for a single session.

title.en: Publish what the agent is for, and what it declines, in onboarding and help text

description.en: Where proportionate, tell users before and during use what the agent can and cannot do: a welcome message or onboarding screen naming its intended uses, a help or FAQ entry listing the subjects it declines, and a hint in the interface when a conversation nears a boundary. Keep the wording in step with the scope statement. Attach screenshots or copies of each piece of guidance with the date it went live.

evidenceHint.en: Screenshots or copies of onboarding, help and in-interface guidance on the agent's purpose and declined subjects, with go-live dates

text.en: Write a welcome or onboarding message naming the agent's intended uses.
Add a help or FAQ entry listing the subjects the agent declines and why.
Show a hint in the interface when a conversation nears a scope boundary, where feasible.
Compare every piece of guidance with the current scope statement before release.
Capture each piece of guidance as published, with its go-live date.

title.en: Log declined out-of-scope requests by topic and report attempt frequency for the period

description.en: Have every declined request write a log entry with the matched subject, the session, whether it was a repeat and whether the repeated-attempt rule fired, keeping no more of the conversation than the logging policy allows. At the end of each period, produce a report of attempts per subject, repeat rates and new themes that matched no defined subject. Attach the report and the log query behind it.

evidenceHint.en: Period report of out-of-scope attempts per declined subject, with repeat counts and unmatched themes, plus the log query that produced it

text.en: Write a log entry for each declined request with the subject matched and the session.
Flag the entries where the repeated-attempt rule fired.
Query the log at period end for attempts per subject and repeat rates.
List themes from declined requests that matched no defined subject.
Save the report together with the query used to produce it.

title.en: Revise the declined-topic list and redirection rules from the period's out-of-scope patterns

description.en: Read the period's frequency report alongside any incidents or complaints that involved scope, and decide for each subject whether to tighten detection, loosen a boundary that blocks legitimate requests, add a newly seen theme or reword the redirection message. Have engineering apply each change, and write down the rationale and the pattern it answers. Attach the change log with its rationale.

evidenceHint.en: Change log of scope boundary updates, each citing the attempt pattern or incident behind it, with the rule before and after

text.en: Compare the frequency report with the previous period for rising subjects and new themes.
Check whether legitimate in-scope requests were wrongly declined in the period.
Decide per subject whether to tighten, loosen, add or reword the boundary.
Hand each change to engineering and confirm it is live in production.
Enter each change in the change log with its rationale and the pattern it answers.

templates.title: Each agent-specific high-risk output in the taxonomy is detected and met with its set response
templates.description: The risk taxonomy names high-risk outputs particular to this agent and its domain, beyond generic harm, and each one has detection logic, a severity threshold and a defined response — block the output, modify it, or escalate it to human review — with every detection logged. The mapping from category to detector and response is kept in one table and tested against the current taxonomy.
templates.defaultOwnerHint: AI Risk Owner / AI Platform Engineering Lead
templates.objective: To make every high-risk output the taxonomy names for this agent trigger a detector and the response its severity calls for, so none reaches a user or takes effect unhandled.
templates.successCriteria:
Every agent-specific high-risk category in the current taxonomy has at least one detector with a configured severity threshold.
Each category has a defined response at each severity level — block, modify or escalate — and the configuration applies it automatically.
Each detection is logged with its category, severity, score and the response applied.
Seeded outputs for every category trigger the mapped response in testing, and categories added to the taxonomy in the period are mapped.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the current risk taxonomy and the list of agent-specific high-risk categories drawn from it, with severities and examples.
Obtain the mapping table from category to detector, threshold and response, and the classifier, rule and prompt configuration that implements it.
Obtain the detection log for the period and the results of the organisation's seeded-output tests.

Analysis:
Reconcile the taxonomy with the mapping table to find agent-specific categories lacking a detector, a threshold or a response.
For a sample of categories spanning every severity level, submit crafted outputs or prompts that should trigger them, and compare the observed response with the mapped one.
Sample detections from the log and confirm each recorded response matches the mapping for its category and severity.
Check that escalated detections in the sample arrived in the human-review queue.
Compare the mapping's change history with the taxonomy's for categories added or changed in the period.

Output:
A category-by-category table of detector, threshold, mapped response and observed response.
A list of unmapped categories, and of detections whose logged response differs from the mapping.
A list of taxonomy changes not yet reflected in the mapping.

title.en: List the high-risk outputs the risk taxonomy names for this agent's domain, with severities

description.en: From the organisation's risk taxonomy, extract the categories specific to this agent and what it does — for a lending agent, quoting terms it is not authorised to offer; for a clinical intake agent, suggesting a diagnosis — leaving aside the generic harms the harmful-output filter already covers. Give each its severity level and example outputs, and raise with the taxonomy owner any agent-specific risk that has no entry yet. Attach the dated list.

evidenceHint.en: Dated list of agent-specific high-risk output categories drawn from the taxonomy, each with its severity, example outputs and taxonomy version

text.en: Read the current risk taxonomy and mark the categories particular to this agent.
Leave out generic harm categories already handled by the harmful-output filter.
Give each category its taxonomy severity and write example outputs for it.
Raise gaps with the taxonomy owner where an agent-specific risk has no entry.
Date the list and note the taxonomy version it was drawn from.

title.en: Map each agent-specific taxonomy category to a detector and a severity threshold

description.en: For every category on the list, choose how it will be recognised — a classifier, a rule over the output or the action it proposes, a check against reference data such as the products the agent may quote, or defensive prompting — and set the score or condition at which each severity level is reached. Keep the mapping in one table naming category, detector, threshold and where its configuration lives. Attach the mapping table and the detector configuration.

evidenceHint.en: Mapping table from taxonomy category to detector and per-severity threshold, with the classifier, rule or prompt configuration it points to

text.en: Pick a detector type for each category on the agent-specific list.
Set the score or condition that marks each severity level for that category.
Write the mapping table naming category, detector, threshold and configuration location.
Try each detector on the example outputs written for its category before go-live.
Store the table under version control beside the detector configuration.

title.en: Assign a block, modify or escalate response to each taxonomy category at each severity level

description.en: Extend the mapping table with the response each detection triggers. Decide per category and severity whether the output is blocked and replaced with a safe message, modified in real time by redaction, rewriting or an added warning where the deployment calls for it, or escalated to the human-review queue. Configure the responses to run automatically and to write a log entry for every detection. Attach the completed table and the response configuration.

evidenceHint.en: Mapping table giving the response per category and severity, and the configuration that blocks, modifies or escalates automatically

text.en: Decide per category and severity whether the output is blocked, modified or escalated.
Write the safe message a user sees when an output is blocked.
Configure the redaction, rewrite or warning used for modified outputs, where proportionate.
Point escalated detections at the existing human-review queue, not a new channel.
Configure every response to write a detection log entry with category and severity.

title.en: Export the period's agent-specific detection log and check every entry names its response

description.en: At the end of each period, export the detection log for the agent-specific categories, confirm every entry carries the category, severity, score and the response that ran, and list entries where the response is missing or differs from the mapping. Pass the escalation count to the human-review owner and the totals by category to whoever monitors risk in production. Attach the export summary and the list of exceptions.

evidenceHint.en: Period export of agent-specific detections with counts by category, severity and response, and the entries missing or mismatching a response

text.en: Export the period's detection log entries for agent-specific categories.
Count the entries by category, severity and response applied.
List entries with no response or a response that differs from the mapping.
Send escalation counts to the human-review owner and category totals to risk monitoring.
Open a fix with an owner for each exception found.

title.en: Test each agent-specific category with seeded outputs and confirm the mapped response fires

description.en: Once a year, build test cases for every category at each severity level — outputs, or prompts designed to produce them, including paraphrased and partial versions a narrow rule could miss — run them against the production configuration, and compare the response that fired with the mapping table. Reconcile the taxonomy with the table for categories added since the last test that have no mapping. Attach the test cases, the results and the fixes.

evidenceHint.en: Seeded test cases per category and severity with expected and observed responses, unmapped categories found, and the fixes agreed

text.en: Write seeded outputs or prompts for every category at each severity level.
Include paraphrased and partial variants that a narrow rule could miss.
Run the cases against the production configuration and capture the response that fired.
Compare each observed response with the mapping table and flag mismatches.
Reconcile the taxonomy with the table for categories added since the last test.

templates.title: Agent output arrives sanitised wherever it is rendered, run or parsed, with untrusted content labelled
templates.description: Before agent output reaches a browser, a terminal, a drafted document or another system, it is encoded or stripped for that destination, structured output is checked against a schema, and unsafe links are blocked or rewritten. Content from untrusted sources is labelled apart from the agent's own words and handled more strictly, and where proportionate output is scanned for embedded attack payloads. Applies to agents that generate code, text or speech.
templates.defaultOwnerHint: Application Security Lead / Front-end Engineering Lead
templates.objective: To stop agent output carrying script, shell, link or data injection into the place it is shown or used, and to let users tell untrusted content from the agent's own words.
templates.successCriteria:
Every destination where agent output is rendered, run or parsed is inventoried with the sanitisation it requires.
Each destination applies its encoding, escaping or schema check, and links outside the allowed schemes and domains are blocked or rewritten.
Content from retrieval, tools or third parties carries a source label in the interface and is sanitised at least as strictly as the agent's own text.
This quarter's payload tests found every payload inert at each destination, or a fix is recorded for each that was not.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the inventory of output destinations with the sanitisation each one requires.
Obtain the encoding, escaping, schema-validation, content security policy and link-handling configuration for each destination.
Obtain the source-labelling implementation and screenshots of labelled content.
Obtain the quarter's payload test results and, where adopted, the output-scanning rules and their hit log.

Analysis:
Compare the inventory with the product's rendering and integration points to find destinations it omits.
For each destination, have the agent emit a set of payloads — script tags, event handlers, image links to outside hosts, disallowed link schemes, shell metacharacters in displayed commands, malformed structured output — and observe whether each arrives inert.
Seed a retrieved document and a tool result with instructions and markup, and confirm both are labelled and sanitised when shown.
Sample scanning hits from the quarter and confirm each led to the configured action.

Output:
A destination-by-payload matrix showing each payload inert or executed.
A list of untrusted content found shown without a label.
A list of destinations missing from the inventory and of payloads that executed, each with its fix.

title.en: Inventory every place agent output is rendered, executed or parsed by another system

description.en: Trace agent output to every destination that interprets it: the chat interface's markdown or HTML renderer, emails and documents the agent drafts for others to open, commands shown for a user to copy into a terminal, link previews, and APIs or workflows that parse its JSON or YAML. Note for each destination the interpreter involved and the kind of injection it is exposed to. Attach the dated inventory.

evidenceHint.en: Dated inventory of output destinations, naming the interpreter at each and the injection type it is exposed to

text.en: List each interface that renders agent output and the renderer it uses.
Add emails, documents and messages the agent drafts for other people to open.
Include commands offered for copying and structured output parsed by other systems.
Note the injection each destination is exposed to: script, link, shell or data.
Date the inventory so the quarterly payload test can compare against it.

title.en: Configure contextual encoding, schema checks and link rules for each output destination

description.en: Apply the sanitisation each inventoried destination needs: render markdown with raw HTML disabled or through an allowlist sanitiser, escape output in templates, send a content security policy, quote or warn on shell metacharacters in commands offered for copying, validate structured output against a strict schema before it is passed on, and block or rewrite links whose scheme or domain is not allowed, including image links that would fetch from unknown hosts. Attach the configuration per destination.

evidenceHint.en: Per-destination sanitisation configuration: renderer settings, escaping, content security policy, schema validators and link allowlist or rewrite rules

text.en: Disable raw HTML in the markdown renderer or pass it through an allowlist sanitiser.
Turn on auto-escaping in every template that inserts agent output.
Send a content security policy on pages that display agent output.
Validate structured output against a strict schema before any system consumes it.
Block or rewrite links and images whose scheme or domain is not on the allowlist.

title.en: Label retrieved, tool-returned and third-party content apart from the agent's own text

description.en: Tag every piece of content with its source as it enters a response — the agent's own generation, the organisation's documents, a tool or web result, a third party's message — and carry that tag through to the interface, where untrusted sources get a visible marker. Apply stricter sanitisation to untrusted content, such as stripping links and markup, and never present it as the agent's own statement. Attach screenshots and the tagging code or configuration.

evidenceHint.en: Screenshots showing untrusted content marked in the interface, and the code or configuration that tags its source and applies stricter handling

text.en: Define the source tags and which of them count as untrusted.
Attach a tag to content from retrieval, tools, web results and third parties.
Show a visible marker on untrusted content wherever it is displayed.
Apply stricter sanitisation to untrusted content before it is rendered.
Capture screenshots of each marker as users see it.

title.en: Scan outgoing agent responses for embedded instructions, command payloads and obfuscated exploits
